# Review: `cronwell/dispatcher.py`

## The code as written can't produce the attached trace — check this before trusting it

Walk through `_materialize_due`:

```python
now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)              # aware
horizon = now + timedelta(seconds=self._tick_s * 2)   # aware
for schedule in self._schedules.list():
    fire_at = next_run_at_from_row(schedule)   # naive — see below
    if fire_at > horizon:                      # naive vs aware
        continue
```

`next_run_at_from_row` calls `next_run_at(Schedule.from_row(schedule_row))` with no `after` argument. Per the models review, `next_run_at` then anchors on `datetime.utcnow()` — a **naive** datetime — and every value it returns (`minute`) inherits that naiveness. So `fire_at` is naive, `horizon` is aware, and `fire_at > horizon` raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes` on the very first schedule evaluated, every tick.

That exception propagates out of `_materialize_due` into `_loop`'s `except Exception: metrics.count("dispatcher.tick_error")` — meaning every real tick should fail immediately, before scanning any schedules past the first, before materializing anything, and before `_balance_capacity` ever runs. That's inconsistent with the trace, which shows `schedules_scanned≈41000` and non-zero `materialized` counts on nearly every row. Either the trace was captured against a different build than the code under review, or something upstream of what's shown here changes `next_run_at`'s naiveness — but as this file and `models.py` stand together, the comparison should crash every tick. This needs to be resolved before using the trace as evidence of the lock-contention pattern below — the pattern is plausible and worth investigating on its own merits, but the trace shouldn't be taken as proof this code currently runs successfully in production.

Fixing the underlying issue also matters beyond the crash: even once `next_run_at` returns an aware datetime, it still ignores `schedule.timezone_name` entirely (flagged in the models review) — so `_materialize_due`, the module that actually turns that into production scheduling decisions for ~41,000 schedules, would silently compute every fire time in UTC regardless of what timezone each schedule declares.

## `_materialize_due` rescans every schedule from scratch, every tick, with no caching — this is the real lock-contention driver

`self._schedules.list()` returns literally every schedule row (no due-time filter is possible at the SQL level — the `schedules` table has no `next_fire_at` column to index on), and `next_run_at_from_row` is called **unconditionally**, before the `due` check, for every one of them. `next_run_at`'s algorithm is a minute-by-minute linear scan capped at just under a year (per the models review) — cheap for common cron patterns that fire within minutes or hours, but potentially hundreds of thousands of iterations for sparse (e.g. annual) expressions. Since nothing caches a schedule's next fire time between ticks, and `after` is never passed, this full cost is paid again from scratch every 5 seconds, forever, for all ~41,000 schedules.

The trace itself rules out simpler explanations for the periodic multi-second stalls. Compare the `due=0` ticks: most take 0.08–0.30s (t+115, t+475, t+565, t+675, t+1035), but **t+260 has `due=0, materialized=0` and still takes `lock_held_s=4.67`** — proving the expensive part isn't proportional to how many schedules are due or how many runs get materialized. That's consistent with a subset of schedules having cron expressions whose from-scratch `next_run_at` search is periodically expensive depending on how far `now` sits from their next real occurrence — exactly the failure mode you'd expect from recomputing an uncached, unbounded linear search every tick. The ~85s spacing between spikes (t+5, 90, 175, 260, 345, 430...) is a fixed, suspiciously regular interval that's worth targeted profiling (per-schedule timing, or logging any single `next_run_at` call that takes more than a few milliseconds) rather than guessing further from this data alone — but the structural cause (full rescan, no caching, unbounded per-schedule search cost) is enough on its own to guarantee this class of problem will get worse as the schedule count grows.

This matters specifically because all of it runs **inside `with self._lock`**, the same lock `enqueue_manual` needs. The trace's own note confirms the consequence: manual triggers queue up (`trigger_calls_waiting` up to 7) exactly during these slow ticks. A user-facing "run this job now" request can block for several seconds behind a background scan that has nothing to do with their request.

## `_balance_capacity` sleeps while holding the lock

```python
if active >= capacity:
    metrics.gauge("dispatcher.saturation", active - capacity)
    self._stop.wait(self._tick_s)
```

This call sits inside `_loop`'s `with self._lock:` block. When the fleet is saturated, the dispatcher blocks for up to a full `tick_s` **while still holding the lock** — on top of the `tick_s` the outer loop already waits between iterations. Under saturation, that's up to `2 * tick_s` of continuous lock ownership, during which `enqueue_manual` is blocked the entire time. Reusing `self._stop` (an `Event` meant for shutdown signaling) as a general sleep-with-backoff primitive is what causes this — a saturation backoff should release the lock before sleeping, the same way the outer loop's own `_stop.wait` already does outside the lock.

## `_balance_capacity`'s docstring overstates what it does

> "Refuse new materialization when the fleet is saturated."

`_loop` calls `_materialize_due()` *before* `_balance_capacity()`. By the time saturation is detected, this tick's materialization has already happened unconditionally — `_balance_capacity` only delays the *next* tick's call to `_materialize_due`, and (per above) does so by blocking the lock rather than by actually gating insertion. Nothing here "refuses" the materialization that just occurred. The docstring's own admission ("a burst between read and insert can overshoot") undersells this — it's not just a narrow read/insert race, it's that capacity is checked strictly after-the-fact, once per tick, with a blunt full-stop/full-go response rather than a bound on how much a single tick materializes.

## Redundant per-schedule dedup query, on top of a unique index that already handles it

```python
existing = self._runs.list(job_id=schedule["job_id"], scheduled_for=fire_at)
if existing:
    continue
```

The schema already enforces `UNIQUE (job_id, scheduled_for)`, and the schema's own comment says as much: "the dedup index is why a duplicate materialization is an IntegrityError and not a second row." This pre-check duplicates that guarantee with an extra `JobRunStore.list()` round-trip for every due schedule, under the lock, for no correctness benefit — the unique index plus `insert()`'s existing `IntegrityError` handling already prevents the double row. Dropping the pre-check and relying on the constraint (which the code already needs to handle anyway) removes real per-tick DB traffic without changing behavior.

## `_materialize_due`'s insert result is discarded — the metric over-reports

```python
self._runs.insert(run.to_row())
metrics.count("dispatcher.materialized")
```

Per the storage-layer review, `insert()` returns `None` on any constraint violation, including the dedup collision the schema comment describes as an expected, routine outcome. This code counts `dispatcher.materialized` regardless of whether the row actually landed — so a dedup collision on this path silently inflates the metric, and anyone trusting it to reconcile "how many runs did we create this tick" gets a number disconnected from reality. Contrast with `enqueue_manual`, a few lines below, which does check the return value before counting — that's the pattern this call should follow too.

## `_balance_capacity`'s active-run count fetches full rows just to `len()` them

```python
active = len(self._runs.list(state=RunState.LEASED.value)) + len(
    self._runs.list(state=RunState.RUNNING.value)
)
```

`JobRunStore.list()` has no `LIMIT` and selects every column (per the storage review) — this pulls and materializes every leased/running row in the whole table into Python, twice, just to count them, every tick, under the lock. A `SELECT COUNT(*)` would do the same job without transferring row data the caller never uses; at any meaningful fleet size this is another avoidable contributor to lock hold time.

## Exceptions are swallowed into a bare counter, with no logging

```python
except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001 - the loop must survive a tick
    metrics.count("dispatcher.tick_error")
```

No `logger.exception(...)`, no traceback, nothing beyond an incremented counter — for either the (likely) `TypeError` above or any other failure (a `StorageError`, a raw psycopg exception, anything). This is exactly the kind of catch that would let the naive/aware datetime bug run in production indefinitely: on-call sees `dispatcher.tick_error` climbing with zero information about why, and — worth noting explicitly — if `_materialize_due` crashes before `_balance_capacity` runs, saturation backpressure is *also* silently disabled for as long as this persists, since that function never executes past the crash point.

## Leader election is asserted in the docstring but not implemented here

> "a cluster elects a single active dispatcher through the leader lease in storage"

Nothing in this file acquires, renews, or checks a leader lease — no such store is imported or referenced. If that logic lives entirely in whatever constructs and calls `Dispatcher.start()`, that's fine, but it's worth confirming that module actually fences a demoted leader (stops the thread, not just stops calling `start()` again) — because the check-then-insert race in `_materialize_due` (list-then-insert, not atomic beyond the unique index) is precisely the failure mode two concurrently active dispatchers would hit, and the unique-index fallback would only prevent duplicate rows, not duplicate wasted work or duplicate metric counts.

## Minor

- `enqueue_manual` correctly checks its own `insert()` return value before counting the metric — good, and a useful contrast to fix `_materialize_due` against. But a `None` return (e.g., from an invalid `job_id` that violates a foreign key, per the storage review's blanket `IntegrityError` handling) is indistinguishable from a benign duplicate — a user hitting "run now" on a bad `job_id` gets a silent `None`/no-op rather than a clear error.
- `active >= capacity` counts leased/running runs across the whole fleet, including any still in flight on draining workers, while `capacity` excludes draining workers' capacity from the sum — conservative (makes saturation trigger sooner during a drain), not incorrect, but worth knowing it's not symmetric.
- `metrics.gauge("dispatcher.saturation", ...)` only fires inside the saturated branch — if the metrics backend retains the last value between emissions, a dashboard could show a stale saturation reading long after the fleet recovers, since there's no corresponding "healthy" emission on the non-saturated path.
- `next_run_at_from_row` imports `Schedule` locally on every call instead of alongside the existing top-level `from cronwell.models import ... next_run_at`. Harmless (import caching), but there's no reason for the inconsistency.

## What to check next
- Whichever module owns `current_config()`/leader-lease election and constructs `Dispatcher` — confirm fencing behavior and reconcile the naive/aware `next_run_at` question against `models.py` before trusting the attached trace.
- Whether `schedules` ever gets a precomputed/indexed `next_fire_at` column — that's the real fix for the O(all schedules) rescan, not just optimizing the current loop.

# Review: `cronwell/api_handlers.py`

## The stated error contract doesn't match what storage actually returns `None` for

> "Storage returning None maps to 404."

Every `create()` follows this literally:
```python
inserted = self._store.insert(model.to_row())
if inserted is None:
    return Response.not_found("job")
```

But per the storage-layer review, `insert()` returns `None` for *any* `IntegrityError` — duplicate key, foreign-key violation, NOT NULL violation, or check-constraint violation, all collapsed into the same `None`. None of those are "the resource wasn't found" — there was never a resource to find; this is a **write** that failed. Concretely:

- `POST /api/v1/schedules` with a `job_id` that doesn't exist (FK violation) returns `Response.not_found("schedule")` — telling the client the schedule they're trying to create doesn't exist, which is nonsensical, and hiding the real problem (the referenced job doesn't exist).
- `POST /api/v1/jobs` with a duplicate unique key returns the same 404, when a 409 (or 422) would actually communicate what happened.
- A NOT NULL or check-constraint violation — genuinely a validation problem, exactly the kind of thing the docstring says should be 422 — also comes back as 404.

`update()` has the same problem in a milder form: `None` there is legitimately "row not found" *or* "constraint violated by the changes" (e.g., PATCHing a schedule's `job_id` to a nonexistent job), and the handler can't tell which — a schedule that obviously exists (the client has its id) gets reported as "not found" when the real issue is the new `job_id` they supplied.

This needs storage's `insert`/`update` to distinguish these cases (per the earlier review's recommendation) before this layer can map them correctly — right now the API contract is internally consistent with the code but built on a false premise about what `None` means.

## Every `get`/`update`/`delete`/`RunControlHandlers` method crashes on a malformed `id`

```python
row = self._store.get(int(request.params["id"]))
```

This pattern — `int(request.params["id"])` with no guard — appears unguarded in all 10 CRUD handler classes' `get`, `update`, `delete` methods, plus `RunControlHandlers.trigger`, `cancel`, and `tail`. Two ways a client-supplied path param breaks this:
- The param is missing → `KeyError`, uncaught here.
- The param isn't a valid integer (`"abc"`, empty string, a float-looking string) → `ValueError`, uncaught here.

Both are ordinary client-input mistakes that the module's own error contract says should be a 422, but nothing in this file catches them — they propagate as raw, unhandled exceptions. That's over 30 call sites with the same gap. A single small helper (`parse_id(request) -> int | Response`) used consistently would close all of them at once.

## `list()` endpoints are unbounded, and unknown filter keys crash instead of returning 4xx

```python
filters = {key: value for key, value in request.params.items() if key != "id"}
return Response.ok(self._store.list(**filters))
```

Two separate problems, both directly relevant to "large tables":

1. **No pagination anywhere.** `GET /api/v1/job_runs` with no query params runs `SELECT * FROM job_runs ORDER BY id` with no `LIMIT`, fetches every row in the table, and serializes the whole thing into one HTTP response. For `job_runs`, `run_attempts`, and `audit_events` — tables that grow without bound as the scheduler operates (the dispatcher trace alone showed ~41,000 *schedules*; `job_runs` accumulates every fire of every one of them, repeatedly, forever) — this endpoint can trivially return an unbounded response large enough to exhaust memory on the API process, and it requires no special input to trigger: the empty-filter request is the worst case. This needs `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` or cursor pagination at both the storage and API layers before it's safe to expose.

2. **Unknown filter keys aren't handled here.** Per the storage review, `Store.list()` *does* validate filter keys against an allowlist and raises `StorageError` for anything else (unlike `update()`, which doesn't validate at all). This handler never catches `StorageError` — so `GET /api/v1/jobs?bogus=1` raises an uncaught exception instead of the clean 422 the module's contract promises. It's a smaller version of the same "trust storage errors to map themselves" gap as the create/update issue above.

A secondary note: filter values come straight from `request.params` (presumably strings from a query string) with no coercion to the target column's type before being handed to `store.list(**filters)` — worth confirming psycopg/Postgres actually does the implicit cast you'd want for something like `?priority=5` against an `integer` column, rather than silently matching nothing.

## `delete()` has no handling for FK-blocked deletes

Per the storage review, `Store.delete()` methods catch nothing — a `DELETE` blocked by a foreign key (e.g. deleting a `Job` that still has `Schedule` or `JobRun` rows pointing at it) raises a raw `IntegrityError` straight through. This handler doesn't catch it either:
```python
def delete(self, request: Request) -> Response:
    with metrics.timer("api.jobs.delete_ms"):
        if not self._store.delete(int(request.params["id"])):
            return Response.not_found("job")
        return Response.ok({"deleted": True})
```
`DELETE /api/v1/jobs/{id}` for a job with existing schedules gets an unhandled exception instead of a clear 409 ("cannot delete: referenced by N schedules"). This is the storage-layer gap from that review, now confirmed to reach all the way to the HTTP boundary unguarded.

## `cancel()` doesn't actually cancel in-flight execution

```python
def cancel(self, request: Request) -> Response:
    row = self._runs.update(int(request.params["id"]), {"state": "dead"})
```

This writes `state = "dead"` regardless of the run's current state — including `running`, where a worker is actively executing the handler. Per the consumer review, that worker will eventually write its own terminal state back (`SUCCEEDED` on success, or a retry/`DEAD` transition on failure) with no awareness this API call happened — there's no signal here that reaches the running handler process at all. So calling `cancel()` on a `running` run returns 200 with what looks like a successful cancellation, but the handler keeps executing, and its own completion write is likely to silently overwrite the `dead` state moments later. If "cancel" is meant to stop in-flight work, this doesn't do that — it's only meaningful for runs still in `pending`, and nothing here restricts it to that case or documents the distinction. Also note: this uses the raw string `"dead"` instead of `RunState.DEAD.value`, inconsistent with every other module's convention.

## `tail()` is a full unfiltered dump, not a tail

```python
def tail(self, request: Request) -> Response:
    """The most recent runs of a job, newest first."""
    rows = self._runs.list(job_id=int(request.params["id"]))
    return Response.ok(rows[::-1])
```
No limit — this fetches *every* run ever recorded for the job, then reverses the whole list in Python. For a job on a frequent schedule running for months, "tail" returns its entire history, not a bounded recent window, directly contradicting what the name and docstring promise. It's the same unbounded-`list()` problem as above, but the naming actively misleads a caller into thinking it's safe to call unconditionally. Separately: "newest" here means "highest `id`" (insertion order), not necessarily newest by `scheduled_for` — usually the same thing, but worth being explicit about, since backfilled or manually-triggered runs could insert out of chronological schedule order.

## `{'id': None, **request.json()}` doesn't reliably force `id` to `None`

```python
model = Job.from_row({'id': None, **request.json()})
```
If the client's JSON body includes its own `"id"` key (e.g. they round-tripped a GET response into a POST), dict-literal unpacking means the later key wins — `request.json()`'s `id` silently overrides the explicit `None`. In practice this is inert: every `Store.insert()` explicitly lists which fields it pulls from the row and never includes `id` (per the storage review), and the response returns the DB's `RETURNING`-assigned id, not `model.id`. So no client-controlled id actually reaches the database or gets echoed back — but the code reads as if it guarantees `id=None` when it doesn't, which is worth fixing for clarity (`{**request.json(), 'id': None}` would actually guarantee it) even though it's not currently exploitable.

## Minor

- `except (KeyError, TypeError) as error: return Response.invalid(f"missing field: {error}")` — labels every failure "missing field" even when the actual problem is a wrong-typed value (e.g. `validate()`'s `self.capacity < 0` raising `TypeError` when a client sends `"capacity": "five"`) or a malformed body shape (posting a JSON array instead of an object, which fails at the `**request.json()` unpacking step with `TypeError: argument of type 'list' is not a mapping`). The status code lands right (422) but the message is misleading.
- Raw exception text (`f"{error}"`) goes straight into the 422 response body — low risk here, but worth being deliberate about rather than incidental.
- `metrics.timer(...)` wraps the whole method including early validation-failure returns, mixing microsecond validation failures with real DB round trips in the same latency histogram.
- `RunControlHandlers.__init__(self, conn: Connection, dispatcher)` — `dispatcher` has no type annotation, inconsistent with the rest of the module.
- The docstring's auth line ("handled by the middleware before any handler runs") is unverifiable from this file alone — worth checking that middleware actually scopes access by `Namespace.owner_team`, since nothing here enforces per-namespace ownership despite the model having a concept of it.

## What to check next
- Whatever router/`main()` wires these handlers up — does it catch unhandled exceptions (the `int(id)` and `StorageError` gaps above) into a generic 4xx/5xx, or would those currently reach the client as raw tracebacks or bare 500s?
- The auth middleware — does it enforce `owner_team`/namespace scoping, or is any authenticated caller able to CRUD across all namespaces?

# Review: `cronwell/auth_middleware.py`

## The decision cache silently bypasses the admin IP allowlist after first use

```python
_DECISION_CACHE: dict[str, AuthResult] = {}

def check(headers: dict, remote_addr: str) -> AuthResult:
    token = _bearer_of(headers)
    ...
    cached = _DECISION_CACHE.get(token)
    if cached is not None:
        return cached
    ...
    elif entry.role == "admin" and _ALLOWLIST and remote_addr not in _ALLOWLIST:
        result = AuthResult(False)
    else:
        result = AuthResult(True, team=entry.team, role=entry.role)
    _DECISION_CACHE[token] = result
    return result
```

The cache key is `token` alone — `remote_addr` never enters it. The allowlist check only runs on a cache **miss**. So: the first time an admin token is presented from an allowed network address, the result `AuthResult(True, role="admin", ...)` gets cached against that token string. Every subsequent request bearing the *same token*, from *any* IP — including one entirely outside `admin_networks`, e.g. the public internet — hits the cache and is granted admin access without the allowlist ever being consulted again. `_ALLOWLIST` is a network-scoped control; this cache makes the scoping evaporate after one legitimate use.

This is a straightforward network-segmentation bypass for the most privileged role in the system, and it's silent: the bypass path returns the cached `AuthResult` before reaching `metrics.count("auth.admin_outside_allowlist")`, so no counter or log line distinguishes it from an ordinary allowed-network request. Given the audit log shows steady admin-looking traffic in normal operation, an admin token being cached this way is essentially guaranteed quickly after any server instance starts — meaning the allowlist is only ever enforced for each token's very first use per process, and never again. If an admin token is ever exposed outside the allowed network (a proxy log, a compromised laptop inside the network, a copy-pasted curl command), nothing in this code stops it from being replayed from anywhere.

The fix isn't complicated — key the cache on `(token, remote_addr)`, or simply don't cache admin-role decisions, or re-check the allowlist even on a cache hit — but as written, the cache is actively undoing the one IP-based control this module implements.

## Token rotation doesn't take effect without a process restart, and revocation is worse

The module's own comment states the hazard plainly:

> "main() loads the config file after imports, so an import-time read sees the bootstrap defaults unless the environment overrides them."

```python
_CONFIG = current_config()
_TOKEN_TABLE = {entry.token_sha256: entry for entry in _CONFIG.api_tokens}
```

This runs as an import-time side effect, before `main()` has loaded the real config file (per this module's own account — worth confirming exactly against `config_loader.py`'s documented load order, since that's the next module and should state this authoritatively). Independent of that specific ordering question, the design is explicit and admitted in the docstring: "the middleware caches it for the process lifetime, because tokens rotate through a deploy, not through a config reload." `_TOKEN_TABLE` and `_ALLOWLIST` are computed exactly once and never refreshed.

The attached audit log shows exactly the failure mode this produces. Starting at 11:22:07 and continuing for the entire remainder of the excerpt (40+ minutes), a large share of requests fail with `unknown_token`, each annotated "token present in the NEW config file; instance still serving the table resolved at import." This is a live production incident shape: after the June rotation, this instance kept rejecting valid, newly-issued tokens for the whole observed window, with no sign of self-correcting (no periodic reload) — the only fix is restarting the process.

The inverse case is more serious than the outage the log shows. If a token is rotated *out* — because it leaked, or an employee left, or a client was compromised — the same caching means every already-running instance keeps **accepting** that revoked token indefinitely, until it happens to restart. "Rotate this token" as an incident-response action doesn't actually revoke anything fleet-wide; it only stops *new* processes from accepting the old token. That defeats the primary reason rotation exists as a security control. This needs either a real reload mechanism (config-driven, signal-driven, or polling) or, at minimum, an explicit, coordinated restart requirement documented and enforced as part of the rotation runbook — right now nothing in the code or the observed rotation suggests either happened cleanly.

Two independent staleness layers compound this: even if `_TOKEN_TABLE` were made refreshable, `_DECISION_CACHE` would still serve pre-refresh decisions for any token it had already seen (see below) — so both layers need addressing, not just one.

## `_DECISION_CACHE` is an unbounded, plaintext, never-invalidated cache

```python
_DECISION_CACHE[token] = result
```

Several distinct problems stack here:

- **Unbounded growth / DoS.** Every distinct token string ever presented — valid or garbage — gets a permanent entry (`AuthResult(False)` is cached too). There's no TTL, no LRU, no cap. A client sending distinct random bearer tokens in a loop (a buggy retry, or a deliberate attacker) grows this dict forever, with no bound on individual token length either (`_bearer_of` doesn't cap it), so both the *count* and the *size* of entries are attacker-influenced. This is a straightforward, easily triggered memory-exhaustion vector.
- **Plaintext secret retention.** `_TOKEN_TABLE` deliberately stores only `token_sha256` digests — the codebase clearly intends not to hold raw tokens in memory. This cache undoes that: every valid token presented is retained as a live dict key, in plaintext, for the life of the process. A heap dump or memory-inspection tool would recover every bearer token ever used against this instance, defeating the hashing done one line above.
- **Permanent negative caching.** A token tried once before the server's config includes it (e.g., a client racing a config update, or hitting this instance during the exact staleness window described above) gets `AuthResult(False)` cached forever for that exact token string on that instance — even if the underlying config problem is later fixed, that specific token is now permanently rejected by this process until restart.
- **No production escape hatch.** `reset_for_tests()` clears the cache but is explicitly scoped to tests ("production never does"). Given the rotation incident, an equivalent operationally-accessible reset (an authenticated admin endpoint, a signal handler) would at least let ops force stale decisions out without a full restart — right now there's no lever for that in production at all.

## Minor

- `_lookup`'s linear scan uses `hmac.compare_digest` per entry, which is the right instinct for avoiding a timing side-channel on digest comparison — but the loop still returns as soon as a match is found, so total scan time varies with *where* in `_TOKEN_TABLE` the match sits (or doesn't). That's a much narrower leak than comparing without `compare_digest` at all, and requires an attacker who can already produce plausible digests to exploit meaningfully, but it's not fully constant-time end-to-end.
- `_bearer_of` checks both `"authorization"` and `"Authorization"` keys explicitly, which only covers those two exact casings — fine if the framework normalizes headers before this runs, worth confirming it does, since a raw `dict` (per the type hint) offers no such guarantee on its own.
- `check()` mutates `_DECISION_CACHE` with a plain `dict` and no lock. CPython's GIL makes individual `dict` operations atomic, so this doesn't corrupt state today, but two concurrent requests for a brand-new token can both miss the cache and redundantly perform the same lookup — harmless today, but worth knowing this relies on GIL semantics rather than being deliberately safe.
- `_CONFIG = current_config()` running as a bare import-time side effect means merely *importing* this module (e.g. from an unrelated test or a management script) locks in whatever config exists at that moment — the load-order hazard the module's own comment describes is really a symptom of doing config-dependent initialization at import time rather than during an explicit startup step. An explicit `auth_middleware.init(config)` called from `main()` after config load would remove the ambiguity outright instead of documenting it as a known risk.

## What to check in `config_loader.py`
- Its docstring's stated load order — confirm whether `main()` really does load the config file after this module's imports run in every deployment path (not just in theory), and what "bootstrap defaults" actually contains for `api_tokens`/`admin_networks` in that case.
- Whether there's any existing reload/refresh mechanism this middleware could hook into, or whether one needs to be built for both `_TOKEN_TABLE` and `_DECISION_CACHE` to be addressed together.

# Review: `cronwell/config_loader.py`

## `[defaults]` never lands anywhere — verified against `_flatten`

The file's own embedded comment asks that each section be checked: "verify each section above actually lands." Walking `_flatten` against every section in the deployed TOML, all of them map correctly *except* `[defaults]`:

```python
name = f"{section}_{key}" if f"{section}_{key}" in known else key
```

For `[defaults] priority = 5`: the composed name is `"defaults_priority"` — not a known field (the actual field is `default_priority`, singular). It falls back to the bare key `"priority"` — also not a known field. Neither branch matches, so the value is silently dropped. Same for `jitter_s` → `"defaults_jitter_s"` / `"jitter_s"`, neither matching `default_jitter_s`. The mismatch is purely `defaults` (plural, the TOML section) vs. `default_` (singular, the field prefix).

The practical effect: `Config.default_priority` and `Config.default_jitter_s` *always* take their bootstrap values (`5`, `30`) regardless of what's in the file. This is currently invisible because the file's values happen to equal the bootstrap defaults — but it's a live landmine: someone editing `[defaults] priority = 10` expecting it to take effect will get silent no-op behavior with zero error anywhere in the pipeline. This needs either a section rename (`[defaults]` → `[default]`) or a special-case in `_flatten`, plus ideally a check that every parsed TOML key maps to *something*, so a future orphaned key doesn't disappear silently again.

Separately, `[api] request_log = true` has no corresponding `Config` field at all (there's `api_bind` but nothing for `request_log`) — that one gets dropped for a different reason (dead/orphaned config, not a naming bug), but the effect is the same: a value someone deliberately set in the file is silently discarded.

## `load()` treats "file missing" identically to "no file requested" — this is what happened to scheduler-3

```python
if path is not None and Path(path).exists():
    with open(path, "rb") as handle:
        raw = tomllib.load(handle)
    values.update(_flatten(raw))
values.update(_environment_overrides())
```

If `path` is `None`, or points to a file that doesn't exist, `load()` doesn't raise — it silently proceeds as if no file was ever intended, falling back to environment overrides plus bootstrap defaults for everything else, including `api_tokens=()`.

The effective-config diff makes this concrete. Scheduler-3 shows `api_tokens: <0 tokens>`, `admin_networks: ()`, and `retry_backoff_base_ms: 200` — all three at their bare bootstrap-default values, while schedulers 1 and 2 (same deploy tag) show the file's real values (24 tokens, 2 networks, 250). The drift note confirms `load()` *did* run on scheduler-3 — it just silently resolved to "nothing loaded" rather than raising a startup error that would have made the problem impossible to miss. In a system where every deployment is expected to ship a real config file, a missing file at the expected path should fail loudly (raise, refuse to start) rather than quietly downgrading a production instance to zero valid tokens and an empty admin allowlist. Note the `admin_networks=()` result specifically: since the auth middleware's check is `entry.role == "admin" and _ALLOWLIST and remote_addr not in _ALLOWLIST`, an empty `_ALLOWLIST` makes that whole condition short-circuit false — meaning if `api_tokens` had *not* also been empty here, this failure mode would have been fail-*open* (any admin token accepted from any IP) rather than fail-closed. This snapshot happens to be the safer variant only because both fields failed together; that's coincidence, not something the code guarantees.

## Reconsidering `auth_middleware.py` now that `load()`'s replace semantics are visible

`current_config()` always returns whatever `_current` currently is — `load()` doesn't mutate the old `Config` object, it rebinds the module-level name to a new one. That means `current_config()` genuinely is "live" in the sense that calling it *after* a `load()` gets the fresh values — which is exactly what `/configz`'s `dump_effective(current_config())` does, correctly, on every request.

But `auth_middleware.py` doesn't do that. It calls `current_config()` exactly once, at import time, and binds the result to module-level `_CONFIG`/`_TOKEN_TABLE`/`_ALLOWLIST`. Because of how Python name binding works, no later call to `config_loader.load()` — no matter how many times it's called, no matter how correctly it re-reads the file — will ever be visible to those already-bound names in `auth_middleware`. This confirms the earlier finding precisely: whether `auth_middleware` sees the real token table depends entirely on whether `main()` happens to import it *after* calling `load()` — a fact this module cannot settle on its own, since (see below) it doesn't document that ordering, and `main()` hasn't been reviewed yet.

It's also worth being precise about what this module's docstring actually promises, versus what auth_middleware's comment claims. This docstring documents **value precedence** within one `load()` call ("environment variables over the config file over the bootstrap defaults") — it says nothing about *when* `load()` is called relative to other modules being imported. The claim "main() loads the config file after imports" lives only in `auth_middleware.py`'s own comment, unverified and undocumented here. So the uncertainty from the auth-middleware review isn't resolved by this module — it's now clear that resolving it requires reading `main()` directly, since neither module asserts or guarantees the ordering the comment describes.

What *is* now fully clear, independent of that ordering question: even in the best case where `main()` gets the order right at startup, `auth_middleware` still has no way to observe a *later* `load()` call (a hot-reload, a SIGHUP handler, anything) — because it never calls `current_config()` again after import. The "current_config() returns the last loaded object" design this module implements is real and useful, but auth_middleware simply never uses it that way. The same one-shot pattern was already flagged in `retry_policy.py` (`RetryPolicy.from_config()` called once in `Consumer.__init__`) — this looks like a systemic convention problem across the codebase: config consumers cache at construction/import time instead of consulting `current_config()` at use time, silently opting every one of them out of whatever reload capability this module was built to support.

## `retry_backoff_base_ms`: 200 here vs. 250 in `models.py` — confirmed real, and now shown to matter

`models.py` documents `DEFAULT_RETRY_BACKOFF_BASE_MS = 250` with an explicit comment: "config_loader.py keeps its own copy of these values for bootstrap; keep both in sync." This module's actual value is `retry_backoff_base_ms: int = 200`. # Review: `cronwell/metrics.py`

## `timer()`'s docstring is wrong about the one thing that matters: it swallows every exception

```python
@contextmanager
def timer(name: str, tags: dict | None = None):
    """...The emit happens in finally, so a raising block still reports its
    duration; the exception itself is not re-raised past the emit
    only when the block already handled it - a bare raise inside the
    block propagates normally.
    """
    started = time.monotonic()
    try:
        yield
    except Exception:
        timing(name, (time.monotonic() - started) * 1000, _err(tags))
    else:
        timing(name, (time.monotonic() - started) * 1000, tags)
```

Two things are wrong immediately: there's no `finally` anywhere in this code (the docstring's first sentence describes code that doesn't exist), and there's no `raise` anywhere in the `except Exception:` branch either.

That second omission is the real problem, and it's a well-known `contextlib.contextmanager` trap. When an exception is raised inside a `with timer(...):` block, `contextmanager.__exit__` resumes the generator by throwing that exception in at the `yield` point. Here, that lands inside `except Exception:`, which handles it and then — because there's no `raise` — the generator function simply returns. From `__exit__`'s perspective, the generator completed normally after being thrown an exception, which is exactly the signal `contextlib` uses to mean "this exception was handled, suppress it." **The `with` block swallows the exception outright.** Control resumes after the `with` block as if nothing happened — no traceback, no propagation, nothing. The docstring's claim that "a bare raise inside the block propagates normally" would only be true if there *were* a `raise` statement in that branch; there isn't, so nothing ever propagates.

This single bug has a large blast radius given the call-site list, and it changes conclusions from two earlier reviews.

### In `queue_consumer.py`: a raising handler gets reported as `succeeded`, not retried

```python
try:
    handler = self._resolve(job["handler"])
    with metrics.timer("consumer.handler_ms", tags={"job": job["name"]}):
        handler(job["payload"])
except Exception as error:
    ...  # attempt recording, retry decision, dead-lettering
```

If `handler(job["payload"])` raises, that exception is caught and suppressed *inside* the `timer` block — it never reaches `_process`'s own `except Exception as error:`. The `try:` block containing the `with` statement therefore completes without ever seeing an exception, so control falls straight through to the **success path** below it: an attempt row gets inserted with `error: None`, and the run is marked `SUCCEEDED`. A handler that genuinely raised an exception is recorded as having succeeded. None of the retry/dead-lettering logic in `_process`'s `except` clause ever runs for this class of failure.

This needs to be reconciled against the earlier queue-consumer and retry-policy reviews: I had assumed handler exceptions reliably reach the retry path (and the March postmortem, reviewed alongside `retry_policy.py`, describes exactly that — "the retry policy did what it promises: it returned every failed run to the pending set with backoff"). Per this code, a handler that raises should instead be silently misreported as successful, never entering the pending set at all. That's a real tension worth resolving before trusting either account fully — either the March failures weren't manifesting as exceptions caught inside this specific `with` block (e.g., they were hangs rather than raises, or failures surfaced somewhere this timer doesn't wrap), or this suppression behavior is a change that postdates that incident. Either way, as the code stands today, a handler that raises is worse off than one that hangs: hangs at least leave the run visibly `running` for the reaper to eventually catch; a raise gets actively misreported as success.

### In `api_handlers.py`: every uncaught exception I flagged becomes a silent `None` return, not a propagating error

Every CRUD handler wraps its *entire* body in `with metrics.timer(...)`. That means every uncaught-exception bug identified in the API handlers review — the unguarded `int(request.params["id"])` raising `KeyError`/`ValueError`, `list()`'s unknown filter keys raising `StorageError`, `delete()`'s unguarded `IntegrityError` on FK-blocked deletes — no longer propagates as an exception at all. It gets caught and suppressed by the timer, and the handler function falls off the end, implicitly returning `None` instead of a `Response`. That's a worse failure mode than the one I described in that review: instead of a clean (if unhandled) exception with a traceback pointing at the actual bug, whatever calls these handlers (`main()`'s router, not yet reviewed) receives `None` where it expects a `Response` object — any subsequent attempt to read `.status`/`.body` off that `None` fails with a misleading traceback pointing at the router, nowhere near the actual cause. This makes every one of those earlier findings materially harder to diagnose in production than I assessed at the time, and it should be read as an amendment to that review rather than a separate issue.

## The lock-guarded `sendto()` performs synchronous DNS resolution — this explains the March postmortem's other claim

`cfg.metrics_host` is `"statsd.internal"` — a hostname, not an IP literal — and it's passed straight into `sendto()`:
```python
_ensure_socket().sendto(payload, (cfg.metrics_host, cfg.metrics_port))
```
A UDP `sendto()` syscall requires an already-resolved address; when Python is given a hostname string, it performs a synchronous `getaddrinfo()`-style resolution before the actual send. `setblocking(False)` only affects the socket I/O operation itself — it does nothing to make that resolution step non-blocking. So a slow or hung DNS lookup for `metrics_host` stalls `sendto()` regardless of the non-blocking flag, and that call happens *inside* `_lock` — meaning a single stuck resolution serializes every metrics emission across the entire process behind it.

This is precisely the mechanism the March postmortem (reviewed alongside `retry_policy.py`) describes: "the metrics host lost DNS for 40 minutes... every emit blocked on resolution inside the metrics lock." That postmortem's account isn't speculative background anymore — this module's code is a direct, confirmed explanation of it: any handler wrapped in `with metrics.timer(...)` (which, per the call-site list, includes essentially every handler invocation and every API request) would have its exit blocked on the DNS-poisoned lock, making handler execution *appear* to hang from the caller's side even if the handler itself finished — which is exactly consistent with "handler durations ballooned" and "handlers crossed their registration timeouts." The `except OSError: pass` here only protects against a *fast-failing* resolution error (e.g. `gaierror` for NXDOMAIN); it does nothing for a resolution that's merely slow, which is the failure mode that actually occurred. The docstring's promise — "a dropped UDP packet is a lost point, never a stall" — is false in exactly this scenario. Resolving `metrics_host` once (e.g. at config load, or via `socket.connect()` on the UDP socket so the OS resolves it once and caches the destination) rather than on every `sendto()` call would remove this risk.

## The lock protects far more than it needs to

The attached capture's own note says: "the sum of inter-packet gaps is dominated by emit serialization on metrics._lock, not by network time." That's consistent with the design as written: `_lock` wraps the entire `sendto()` call for every emit from every thread in the process — API request handlers, the queue consumer's processing loop, and the dispatcher's tick loop all funnel through one global mutex, with no logical reason to serialize against each other. UDP sockets are safe for concurrent `sendto()` calls without external locking — the kernel handles each send atomically. The only thing that genuinely needs the lock is the lazy `_socket is None` check-and-create in `_ensure_socket()`, which happens once. Narrowing the lock to just that (or better, creating the socket eagerly at module load, removing the need for a lock at all) would eliminate the contention the capture explicitly attributes to this lock, independent of the DNS issue above — the two problems compound (a stuck DNS lookup is bad on its own; a stuck DNS lookup that also blocks every unrelated metric in the process is much worse), but they're separate fixes.

## Minor

- `count`/`gauge`/`timing` interpolate `name` and tag values directly into the statsd wire payload with no escaping. `metrics.timer("consumer.handler_ms", tags={"job": job["name"]})` feeds `Job.name` — an arbitrary, API-controlled string up to 255 characters (per the models review, no charset restriction) — directly into `_tag_suffix`'s output. A job named with an embedded `|`, `:`, or `,` would produce a malformed or multi-field statsd packet. Low severity (this corrupts observability data, not application state), but worth sanitizing given the value is user-controlled.
- `current_config()` is read fresh on every `_send()` call rather than cached at import time — this is worth noting as the one module in this whole series that *doesn't* fall into the stale-config-cache pattern flagged in `auth_middleware.py` and `retry_policy.py`. Not a fix for those modules, but a useful existing example of the right pattern to point them at.

- **API handlers review:** every uncaught-exception finding there (malformed `id` params, unknown `list()` filter keys, unguarded `delete()` FK violations) now needs to be read as "silently returns `None` instead of propagating," not "raises an unhandled exception" — a strictly worse and harder-to-diagnose outcome than what I described at the time.

This sits in tension with the March postmortem's account of bulk retries; worth checking directly against `main()` or a runtime trace whether this suppression predates that incident, since the postmortem's narrative and this code's actual behavior don't obviously agree.

## `freeze_time` reproduces the naive-datetime bug instead of testing around it, and its own default fixture hides the ignored-timezone bug

```python
def freeze_time(monkeypatch, at: str):
    """Freeze models.datetime.utcnow at a naive instant."""
    frozen = datetime.fromisoformat(at)
    class FrozenDatetime(datetime):
        @classmethod
        def utcnow(cls):
            return frozen
    monkeypatch.setattr("cronwell.models.datetime", FrozenDatetime)
    return frozen
```

Storage's documented contract is "callers pass aware datetimes" (per the storage-layer review). This fixture's docstring says, in plain language, that it freezes a **naive** instant — it patches `.utcnow()` specifically, the naive-producing classmethod, and every call site passes a bare `datetime.fromisoformat("2025-06-01T02:59:30")` string with no offset. The fixture doesn't work around `next_run_at`'s naive-datetime bug found in the models review — it's built entirely around it, and would need to change shape (freeze `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`, assert `tzinfo` on the result) to ever catch it or verify a fix. No test in this suite ever constructs a schedule with a non-UTC `timezone_name`, so this bug is undetectable not because of a missing assertion, but because the fixture data itself can't distinguish correct from broken behavior. A single test using `timezone_name="America/New_York"` with an expected offset would have caught this immediately.

Also worth noting: `freeze_time`'s patch (`monkeypatch.setattr("cronwell.models.datetime", FrozenDatetime)`) only affects `cronwell.models`'s own module-level `datetime` name. `dispatcher.py` imports `datetime` independently (`from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone`) and calls `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` directly — this fixture cannot reach that code path at all, so it structurally cannot be reused to reproduce or verify a fix for the naive-vs-aware `TypeError` found in `_materialize_due`.

## `MemoryStore` cannot represent `IntegrityError` at all — confirmed dead by mutation testing

```python
def insert(self, row):
    row = {**row, 'id': self.next_id}
    self.rows[self.next_id] = row
    self.next_id += 1
    return row
```

`MemoryStore.insert()` always succeeds. There's no unique constraint, no foreign key, no NOT NULL, no CHECK — nothing that could ever produce the `None` return the entire storage-layer review was built around. The mutation-testing spot run confirms this directly: "insert(): drop the IntegrityError handler entirely -> no test fails (MemoryStore never raises it)." That try/except block — whose *ambiguity* (collapsing duplicate/FK/NOT-NULL/CHECK violations into one `None`) was the headline finding of the storage review, and which the API-handlers review showed gets mapped to the wrong HTTP status across every `create()`/`update()` handler — has zero test exposure. Not "under-tested" — structurally untestable by this double.

This also means the confirmed, concrete bug from the queue-consumer review — `RunAttemptStore.insert()` with `error=None` on the success path silently failing against the real `run_attempts.error TEXT NOT NULL` column — could never be caught by a test built on `MemoryStore`, since the same call against `MemoryStore` succeeds cleanly and returns a normal row. A test asserting "inserting a successful attempt row round-trips correctly" would pass here and still miss the exact bug that's dropping every successful attempt record in production.

`MemoryStore.update()`'s not-found path (`if entity_id not in self.rows: return None`) is at least *representable* — but no test in this file ever calls `.update()` with a nonexistent id to exercise it. Every one of the ten `test_*_store_crud_with_memory_store` tests only exercises the happy path: insert, get, list, update, delete, get-after-delete — identical shape across all ten resource types, none of them ever asserting on a failure return from any operation.

- **Roundtrip tests** (`test_*_roundtrips_through_a_row`) assert `id` plus exactly one other field. `Job`'s roundtrip test never checks `payload`, `priority`, `enabled`, `namespace`, or `handler` survive `to_row()`/`from_row()`. A regression corrupting any of those fields passes cleanly.
- **Validate tests** (`test_*_validates_its_first_field`) are honestly named — they test exactly and only the *first* validation check in each model's `validate()`. `Job.validate()` also checks `namespace` and `handler`; neither is tested. consumer._runs, consumer._jobs = runs, jobs
Consumer._process(consumer, run)
