## Root cause

The checkout outage was triggered by orders-service deploy v2025.11.04.1 (ticket SHOP-5461), rolled out 14:32:05–14:35:06 per the deploy history, whose production config diff reduced `database.pool.max_connections` from 50 to 10 in the same hunk as an intended `read_timeout_ms` edit. The connection-pool trace shows `size` drop from 50 to 10 at 14:32:30, with `in_use` pinned at 10, `idle` at 0, and `waiters` appearing immediately; `wait_p99_ms` jumps to exactly 5000 ms — the pool's own `acquire_timeout_ms` — and holds there for the rest of the trace. Requests queuing past that 5000 ms ceiling failed with `PoolTimeout` in the orders-service error log and surfaced as 504s in the checkout-gateway access log, with the first burst at 14:35. The client retry trace shows the storefront SDK retrying every 504 up to 3 times with exponential backoff, and the retry-queue metrics show `enqueue_per_s` jumping from 2.1 to 14.8 at 14:33:00 while `dequeue_per_s` stays flat at 2.4 for the rest of the incident — the retries added load to the same 10-connection pool rather than relieving it, growing the backlog from 0 to 4,860 by 15:27:00 without changing the underlying capacity. A competing theory attributed the outage to the cache-3 failure recorded in the cache fleet metrics; that node's `hit_rate` is 0.000 from 13:50:00 through 14:10:00 but returns to 0.930 by 14:11:00 and holds in the normal 0.88–0.96 band through 14:14:00 with no gradual recovery curve, 21 minutes before the pool-size change and with no mechanism connecting a cache node's recovery to a config field named `max_connections` — only the production config diff has both the correct timing and the correct mechanism to match the connection-pool trace.

## Trigger versus vulnerability

The trigger was the `max_connections 50 → 10` line in v2025.11.04.1's production config diff, deployed 14:32:05 per the deploy history, described in the change summary as part of "tune db and http timeouts per capacity review" but contradicting the capacity review's own guidance of a 45-connection minimum. The vulnerability was twofold: no automated check validates a connection-pool size change against a configured minimum before rollout, so a single-line typo reached all 24 production pods; and the deploy's own post-rollout health check sampled error rate over a 60-second window that closed at 14:35:20, 21 seconds before the first 504 burst landed at 14:35:41 — the gate measured customer-facing error rate over too short a window rather than pool saturation, which the connection-pool trace shows was already abnormal at 14:32:30, three minutes before the gate closed clean. Neither gap is specific to this one typo: the same pipeline would pass any pool-sizing mistake, and the same gate would miss any failure mode whose damage takes more than 60 seconds to reach the sampled error rate.

## Detection

An impact-based 5xx alert fired at 14:36 per the on-call chat export, roughly one minute after the first 504 burst. The connection-pool trace shows the pool ceiling breached and `waiters` present from 14:32:30 — nearly four minutes before any alert fired, and before the deploy's own health check window closed at 14:35:20. A faster detection would have needed to alert on pool saturation directly (`waiters > 0` or `wait_p99_ms` at the acquire-timeout ceiling) rather than only on downstream customer-facing error rate; no such alert existed. This is the same failure shape as the deploy's release gate: a signal that was already abnormal for minutes went unmeasured by anything wired to page.

## Resolution

The rollback of v2025.11.04.1 to v2025.11.03.6, completed 15:24:00 per the deploy history, restored `database.pool.max_connections` to 50 and ended new impact in the same minute — it worked because it reverted the exact field the connection-pool trace showed had changed, removing the ceiling that was producing waiters and PoolTimeout failures. The retry-queue backlog did not clear immediately: `enqueue_per_s` drops from 14.8 to 3.0 only at 15:27:00 per the retry-queue metrics, and queue depth falls from a peak of 4,860 to 4,050 to 3,240 over the following two minutes as workers, no longer competing for a starved pool, drained the accumulated jobs.

## Impact

The failure was confined to `POST /api/v1/checkout` and `POST /api/v1/cart/confirm`; GET endpoints (products, orders lookup, session refresh, healthz) stayed under 0.1% error throughout, per the checkout-gateway access log. Checkout error rate ran roughly 38–46% from the first burst at 14:35 through 15:23, per the checkout-gateway access log and the on-call chat's live estimate of "roughly 4 in 10 checkouts failing." Total duration from first burst to rollback was 49 minutes (14:35–15:24), with the retry backlog continuing to drain through 15:29 per the retry-queue metrics. Customer effect included support ticket volume passing 300 (on-call chat export) and a status-page acknowledgment of degraded checkout at 14:52 (on-call chat export).

## Blocking bug: the module won't import

Two dataclasses have fields without defaults following fields with defaults, which raises `TypeError` at class definition time:

- **`JobRun`**: `state: str` has no default but comes after `scheduled_for`, `started_at`, `finished_at` (all default `None`).
- **`QuotaUsage`**: `runs_used` and `runs_rejected` have no defaults but come after `window_start` (default `None`).

Neither class can be instantiated, and `import cronwell.models` fails outright. Fix by reordering fields (defaults last) or giving `state`/`runs_used`/`runs_rejected` explicit defaults.

## Contract violation: validation isn't automatic

The module docstring says "every model validates itself on construction," but `validate()` is a plain method, never called from `__init__` or `__post_init__`. Any code that builds a model and skips the explicit `.validate()` call gets an unvalidated object. Every downstream module needs to call `.validate()` itself — if even one call site forgets, the "always validated" invariant silently breaks. Worth either enforcing this in `__post_init__` or renaming the docstring claim so callers don't trust a guarantee that doesn't exist.

## `next_run_at`: the core arithmetic is wrong

- **`timezone_name` is never used.** `Schedule.timezone_name` exists and is validated for non-emptiness, but `_cron_matches` compares directly against `moment.hour`/`moment.minute` in whatever timezone `after` happens to be in — it never converts using `schedule.timezone_name`. A schedule configured for `America/New_York` fires on UTC clock time, not local time. The docstring's claim that "times are UTC everywhere; see `next_run_at` for the schedule arithmetic" implies this function does the local→UTC conversion. It doesn't.
- **Day-of-week numbering doesn't match cron convention.** `_cron_matches` compares the `dow` field against `moment.weekday()`, where Python's Monday=0, Sunday=6. Standard cron uses Sunday=0 (or 7), Monday=1, ..., Saturday=6. A cron expression like `0 9 * * 1` (intended for Monday in standard cron) matches Tuesday here instead.
- **dom/dow are ANDed, not ORed.** Standard cron semantics: when both day-of-month and day-of-week are restricted (not `*`), a match on *either* fires the job. Here, `_cron_matches` requires *both* to match. An expression like `0 0 1,15 * 1` ("1st and 15th, or every Monday") will fire far less often than a cron-literate caller expects — only when the 1st/15th also lands on the wrong weekday.
- **`datetime.utcnow()` is naive, not UTC-aware**, and deprecated since Python 3.12. If `storage.py` returns timezone-aware datetimes (common with `TIMESTAMPTZ` columns), passing them as `after` and mixing them with the naive default will raise `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes` the first time someone omits `after`. Worth deciding now whether `datetime` fields in this module are naive-UTC or aware-UTC, since nothing enforces either.
- **Boundary semantics are undocumented.** The loop starts checking one minute after `after` truncated to the minute — so a schedule matching exactly `after`'s minute is always skipped. Whether `next_run_at` is inclusive or exclusive of `after` isn't stated, and it matters for any dedup/catch-up logic in the dispatcher.

## Cron field parsing gaps

- `_field_matches` raises a bare `ValueError` (via `int(part)`) for non-numeric input like month names, while the rest of the module raises `ValidationError`. Inconsistent error taxonomy for callers that catch `ValidationError` specifically.
- Range parsing (`"a-b"`) never validates `a <= b` or that both are within `lo`/`hi`; a reversed or out-of-bounds range silently matches nothing rather than raising.
- No wraparound support for ranges like `22-2` (10pm–2am), which some cron dialects support — not necessarily required, but undocumented either way.

## Aliasing hazard in `to_row` / `from_row`

`Job.to_row()` puts `self.payload` directly into the row dict (no copy); `Worker.to_row()` does the same with `self.labels`. `from_row()` similarly stores `row["payload"]`/`row["labels"]` directly on the instance. If `storage.py` mutates the dict it receives (for example, to inject metadata before writing), it will mutate the model's own state, and vice versa. Given payload/labels are the mutable fields, this is a realistic bug for a storage module.

## Validation coverage is inconsistent

Some numeric/string fields are bounds-checked, others of the same kind aren't:

| Validated | Not validated |
|---|---|
| `job_id`, `run_id`, `attempt_no`, `capacity`, `quota_runs_per_hour`, `timeout_s` | `Job.priority`, `Schedule.jitter_s`, `RunAttempt.duration_ms`, `Namespace.retention_days`, `QuotaUsage.runs_rejected`, `JobDependency.offset_s`, `AuditEvent.entity_id` |

Also, `MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES` is defined but never checked anywhere in `Job.validate()` — the constant exists for exactly this purpose and is dead code.

`JobRun.state` is typed as plain `str` even though `RunState` enum exists with the presumably-intended values, and `validate()` never checks that `state` is one of them. Any module writing `job_run.state = "queued"` (a typo, not in the enum) would pass validation silently.

## Smaller notes

- `RunAttempt.error: str` has no default and no `None` option, but presumably a successful attempt has no error. There's no documented convention (empty string vs. otherwise) for "no error," which the run-execution module needs to get right.
- `Job.enabled` defaults to `False`. That's a reasonable safety default, but any creation path that forgets to set it explicitly produces a job that silently never runs.
- `RunAttempt.summary()` omits `error` and `duration_ms` — for an audit trail of failed attempts, the error message is arguably the most important field to have in the log line, and it's dropped.
- The comment tying `DEFAULT_*` constants to a duplicated copy in `config_loader.py` is a drift risk worth checking when that module comes up for review.

## Timestamp contract: violated by the one caller we've already seen

`storage.py` states the contract plainly: "Callers pass aware datetimes." `models.py` states "Times are UTC everywhere" but never says whether that means naive-UTC or aware-UTC — and its only timestamp producer, `next_run_at()`, returns a **naive** datetime (`datetime.utcnow()` has no `tzinfo`).

Trace the path: `next_run_at()` produces a naive datetime → the dispatcher (a later module) presumably assigns it to `JobRun.scheduled_for` → `JobRun.to_row()` passes it through unchanged → `JobRunStore.insert()` sends it to Postgres. Nothing in that chain rejects a naive datetime. Once it reaches a `timestamptz` column, Postgres interprets it using the session's `TimeZone` setting, not UTC — so `scheduled_for` can silently land at the wrong instant, by exactly the server's UTC offset. This is the opposite of what a `timestamptz` column is supposed to buy you.

The contract is enforced in exactly one place: `LeaseStore.record_heartbeat()` checks `if at.tzinfo is None: raise StorageError(...)`. No other write path — `JobRunStore.insert`/`update` (`scheduled_for`, `started_at`, `finished_at`), `WorkerStore.insert` (`last_heartbeat_at`), `QuotaUsageStore.insert` (`window_start`), `AuditEventStore.insert` (`recorded_at`) — does the same check. So the module's central promise ("callers pass aware datetimes") is asserted once and silently unenforced everywhere else, and the one producer of schedule times in the codebase you've shown me violates it by construction.

Fix needs to happen on both sides: `next_run_at()` should return an aware UTC datetime, and this module should validate tz-awareness in one place (for example inside `Connection.execute` or a shared helper) rather than one-off in a single method, so the guarantee actually holds everywhere.

## Error handling of `insert`/`update`

- **All constraint violations collapse to the same `None`.** `IntegrityError` is the base class for `UniqueViolation`, `ForeignKeyViolation`, `NotNullViolation`, and `CheckViolation` alike. Catching it broadly and returning `None` means a duplicate name, a `schedule.job_id` pointing at a job that doesn't exist, and a `NOT NULL` violation are all indistinguishable to the caller. The inline comment ("a duplicate insert is not an error the caller can act on") only makes sense for the unique-violation case; it's silently wrong for the other two.
- **The comment is copy-pasted into `update()` verbatim**, where it makes even less sense — "a duplicate insert" isn't the failure mode of an `UPDATE`. A unique or FK violation on update gets the same misleading treatment.
- **Every other exception type is unhandled.** `StorageError` exists ("a query failed for a non-constraint reason") but nothing in `execute()`, `insert()`, or `update()` ever raises it for that case. A syntax error, a lost connection, a pool timeout, or (see below) a type-adaptation failure propagates as a raw `psycopg` exception. A caller who catches `StorageError` specifically, trusting the class's stated purpose, won't catch these.
- **`insert()` does no field validation before building the query.** `tuple(row[f] for f in (...))` raises a bare `KeyError` if `row` is missing a field, rather than a `StorageError` with a useful message.
- **`insert()`/`update()` never check `rowcount`/`RETURNING` results for silent no-ops versus real failures beyond the `None` case** — for example `record_heartbeat` matches on `hostname = %s`; if no worker with that hostname exists, the `UPDATE` affects zero rows and the method returns `None` with no way for the caller to notice.

## Likely runtime bug: dict parameters aren't JSON-adapted

`JobStore.insert`/`update` pass `row['payload']` (a `dict`) directly as a query parameter; `WorkerStore.insert`/`update` do the same with `labels`. psycopg3 does not automatically adapt a plain Python `dict` to `json`/`jsonb` — it needs an explicit `psycopg.types.json.Json(...)` wrapper (or `json.dumps` into a string, if the column is text-cast). Neither is done here. `json` is imported at the top of the file and never used, which suggests this was meant to happen and got dropped.

If so, every `JobStore.insert`, `JobStore.update` (when `payload` is in `changes`), `WorkerStore.insert`, and `WorkerStore.update` (when `labels` is in `changes`) will raise a `ProgrammingError` at the `cur.execute()` call — a `psycopg` error, not an `IntegrityError`, so it isn't caught by the existing `except IntegrityError` block and leaks straight past the module's error-handling story. Worth verifying against the actual schema/psycopg version, but as written this looks broken for any payload/labels write.

## SQL construction: `update()` doesn't validate its keys, `list()` does

`list()` explicitly checks each filter key against an allow-list of real columns before interpolating it into `f"{key} = %s"`. `update()` builds the identical kind of clause — `f"{key} = %s" for key in sorted(changes)` — **without that check**. Any caller that passes a `changes` dict built from less-trusted input (an API layer forwarding a request body, for instance) can inject arbitrary column names, or worse, a crafted key string, directly into the SQL text. Given `list()` already establishes the pattern of allow-listing columns in this file, `update()` should do the same — this looks like an oversight rather than an intentional trust boundary.

## `job_runs.worker_id`: schema drift across all three layers

`LeaseStore.lease_due_runs` writes to `job_runs.worker_id`, and `record_heartbeat` reads/writes `workers.hostname`. But:

- `models.JobRun` (reviewed last turn) has no `worker_id` field at all.
- `JobRunStore`'s own `insert`/`get`/`list`/`update` never select or return `worker_id`, even though the column is live and mutated by `LeaseStore`.

So a run can be leased (its `worker_id` set) and nothing built on `JobRunStore` — the "normal" CRUD surface for this table — can ever see which worker holds it. Any later module that calls `JobRunStore.get()` to inspect a leased run's owner will get an incomplete row. This needs a field added to `JobRun` in `models.py` and to `JobRunStore`'s column lists, or an explicit note that lease ownership is only visible through `LeaseStore`.

Related: `lease_due_runs`'s `RETURNING id, job_id, scheduled_for` is a narrower shape than every other store's `RETURNING` (which returns the full row). If a caller feeds this result into `JobRun.from_row()` expecting the usual shape, it raises `KeyError` on `started_at`/`finished_at`/`state`.

Also worth flagging: `worker_id` is typed `str` in `lease_due_runs`/`record_heartbeat`, but `Worker.id` (the model's actual primary key) is `int | None`. What's actually stored in `job_runs.worker_id` — the worker's hostname or its numeric id? `record_heartbeat` matches by `hostname`, which suggests "worker_id" here is really a hostname string throughout this module. That's confusing naming at minimum, and a real bug if some other module treats it as `workers.id` for a join or FK.

## No lease expiry visible

`lease_due_runs` sets `state = 'leased'` but records no `leased_at`/lease-expiry timestamp anywhere in this module. If a worker dies mid-lease, nothing shown here can identify or reclaim a stuck `leased` run — worth confirming a later module (dispatcher/reaper) handles this, since storage.py provides no hook for it (no "lease older than N seconds" query alongside `lease_due_runs`).

## Smaller notes

- `list()` has no `LIMIT`/pagination on any table, including `job_runs` and `audit_events`, which are the two most likely to grow unbounded. `lease_due_runs` takes a `limit` param; the generic `list()` doesn't, which is an inconsistent posture within the same file.
- `AuditEventStore.get(entity_id)`/`update(entity_id, ...)` reuse the name `entity_id` for the audit row's own primary key, while `AuditEvent.entity_id` (the model field) refers to a *different* entity's id. Same name, two different meanings, in the same file — an easy source of "which entity_id did I mean" bugs in the API layer.
- Table names `job_dependencys` and `quota_usages` are non-standard pluralizations that don't match `JobDependency`/`QuotaUsage`; not a bug, but worth confirming against the actual migration/schema so this isn't a typo that happens to be consistent within this file.
- `Connection` is explicitly "retry-free" — fine as a documented choice, but it means every caller (dispatcher, API layer) needs its own retry/backoff strategy for transient failures; nothing here provides one.

## Blocking bug: `RunAttemptStore` has no `next_attempt_no`

`_process` calls `self._attempts.next_attempt_no(run["id"])` right after the enabled check — before the handler runs. `RunAttemptStore`, as reviewed in the storage module, only exposes `insert`, `get`, `list`, `update`, `delete`. There is no `next_attempt_no` method anywhere in `storage.py`. Every run that passes the disabled-job check hits `AttributeError` and crashes `_process` before the handler is ever invoked. As written, the consumer cannot process a single run. This needs an implementation added to `RunAttemptStore` (the runbook's "attempt_no derives from the stored attempts, not from memory" confirms it's meant to be a DB-computed value, for example `SELECT COALESCE(MAX(attempt_no),0)+1 FROM run_attempts WHERE run_id = %s`).

## Every successful run silently loses its attempt history

Look at the success path:

```python
self._attempts.insert({
    "run_id": run["id"], "attempt_no": attempt_no,
    "worker_id": self._worker_id, "error": None,
    "duration_ms": duration_ms,
})
```

The schema declares `run_attempts.error` as `text NOT NULL`. Inserting `error=None` violates that constraint, which raises `IntegrityError` — and `RunAttemptStore.insert()` catches `IntegrityError` and returns `None`. `_process` never checks that return value. The net effect: **every successful handler execution silently fails to record its attempt row**, with no exception surfacing anywhere. `run_attempts` ends up containing failure rows only; success runs have zero attempt history, forever. This is the exact "error handling of insert" gap from the storage-module review turning into a concrete production bug — a constraint violation and a genuine application bug look identical (`None`) to this caller, and this caller doesn't even check for that.

Combined with `models.RunAttempt.error: str` having no `None`/empty-string convention (flagged in the models review), this confirms the models module never settled on how "no error" should be represented, and the consumer guessed wrong for the schema that was actually built.

## Reaper doesn't write the synthetic attempt row it documents

`Reaper`'s docstring promises: "A run in state running with no attendant heartbeat for the grace window is marked failed **with a synthetic attempt row**, so the run history shows the loss." The actual `sweep()`:

```python
rows = self._conn.execute(
    "UPDATE job_runs SET state = 'failed' WHERE state = 'running' AND worker_id IN (...) RETURNING id",
    (self.GRACE_S,),
)
```

only updates `job_runs.state`. `Reaper` never imports or instantiates `RunAttemptStore`, and no `run_attempts` row is ever inserted. This directly matches the runbook's own complaint: operators say "the reaper section above contradicts that promise" (the "never zero times silently" promise from the original design proposal) — and now you can see the concrete mechanism: the reaper doesn't even leave the audit trail its own docstring claims it does, so there's no `run_attempts` evidence that the run was ever attempted at all. This isn't just a documentation mismatch; it's the specific gap operators have already built a manual checklist to work around.

## Delivery contract is self-contradictory, and the idempotency flag is dead

The module docstring states the contract precisely: a crash between ack and handler completion is **at-most-once** — "the run is finalized by the reaper, not redelivered." That's real and matches `sweep()`'s behavior (mark failed, no re-enqueue). But:

- The original design promise, per the runbook, was "the scheduler may run a job twice, never zero times silently" — i.e., **at-least-once**. The mid-flight-crash path, as implemented, can silently drop non-idempotent work (worse, with no attempt row per the previous finding, there's no evidence it happened at all). Operators have already flagged this contradiction; it isn't hypothetical.
- Meanwhile, the retry-on-exception path is effectively **at-least-once**: `self._retry.decide(attempt_no)` runs unconditionally on any handler exception and, if not `give_up`, reschedules through the pending set for redelivery. Nothing in `_process` consults `HandlerRegistration.idempotent`. The catalog confirms this directly: "roughly a third of the registered handlers declare idempotent = false... The registration field is informational today: no scheduler component reads it." A non-idempotent handler (one that "appends to an external ledger on every call") that raises partway through — after the append already happened — gets retried exactly like an idempotent one, risking a duplicate ledger entry.

So the system delivers neither of its stated guarantees consistently: it's at-most-once (with silent, unrecorded loss) on worker death, and effectively at-least-once (with unguarded duplication risk) on handler exceptions — and the one piece of data that could inform a safer choice (`idempotent`) is loaded into a table and never read by this module, which doesn't even import `HandlerRegistrationStore`.

## `_resolve` bypasses the handler catalog entirely

`_resolve` takes `job["handler"]` — a free-text string validated only for length in `Job.validate()` — and does a raw `importlib.import_module` + `getattr`. It never checks the `handler_registrations` table. Two consequences:

- **No allow-list.** Anything with a `module:function` shape that's importable in the worker's process gets executed, whether or not it was ever registered, reviewed, or approved via the catalog. If job creation is reachable by less-trusted callers (a namespace's API access, for example), this is a real code-execution surface, not just a code-quality note.
- **No timeout enforcement.** `handler_registrations.timeout_s` is defined per handler (60s to 3600s in the catalog) but nothing in `_process` bounds the call to `handler(job["payload"])`. A hung handler blocks that worker's `_process` call indefinitely.

## No return-value checks on the ack/finalize updates

None of the four `self._runs.update(...)` calls in `_process` (ack to RUNNING, dead-on-disabled, dead-on-give-up, succeeded) check whether the update actually returned a row. If any of them silently fails — a constraint violation swallowed by `JobRunStore.update()`'s `except IntegrityError: return None`, or the run row having been deleted concurrently — `_process` proceeds as if it succeeded. The whole point of "ack first" is to keep a lease-holder's view of run state in sync with the database so a duplicate lease can't double-run it; an unchecked, silently-failed ack undermines exactly that guarantee.

## Disabled job and missing job produce the same signal

```python
if job is None or not job["enabled"]:
    self._runs.update(run["id"], {"state": RunState.DEAD.value})
    metrics.count("consumer.skipped_disabled")
    return
```

`job is None` means `job_runs.job_id` points at a job that no longer exists — a dangling reference, and a much more alarming condition than "someone disabled this job." Both produce `state=DEAD`, the same `consumer.skipped_disabled` metric, and (per the earlier NOT-NULL finding pattern) no attempt row explaining why. On-call has no way to distinguish "expected, job was turned off" from "a job was deleted while runs were still scheduled against it" from metrics or run history alone.

## `HandlerNotFound` spends retry budget on an error retries can't fix

The `try` block wraps both `self._resolve(...)` and the handler call, so a bad `handler` path (missing module, missing function, wrong format) raises `HandlerNotFound`, which is caught by the same generic `except Exception` as a legitimate transient runtime failure. It goes through `self._retry.decide(attempt_no)` and gets retried like any other failure, even though re-importing the same broken path will never succeed. This burns through the retry budget (and produces repeated attempt rows / alerts) for what is really a permanent configuration error that should fail straight to `DEAD` on the first attempt.

## Reaper misses workers that never sent a first heartbeat

```sql
WHERE last_heartbeat_at < now() - interval '%s seconds'
```

If `last_heartbeat_at IS NULL` (a worker that died before its first heartbeat, per the schema's nullable `timestamptz`), the comparison evaluates to `NULL`, not `TRUE`, so that worker's `hostname` is excluded from the sweep's `IN (...)` subquery. Any run leased to a worker that crashes before ever heartbeating stays `running` forever — the reaper can never claim it.

## No way to interrupt a stuck handler

`stop()` only flips a flag checked at the top of `run_forever`'s loop. There's no timeout and no cancellation on `handler(job["payload"])`, so a hung handler blocks that check indefinitely — a graceful-shutdown request can't take effect until the handler returns on its own, and the rest of the leased batch (up to `batch - 1` other runs) sits un-processed in the meantime.

## Context: none of the recent history touched these contracts

The attached log shows 40 commits on this file, many labeled "harden," "post-incident," or "review follow-up," but the log note is explicit: none of them changed the ack-ordering, delivery, or idempotency behavior under review here. Worth treating that as a signal — this file has absorbed a lot of churn without anyone addressing the structural issues above, so incremental patches on top of the current design are unlikely to close them; they need direct fixes to the ack/attempt/reaper flow and an explicit decision on the at-most-once vs. at-least-once question before the `idempotent` flag can mean anything.

## Reconciling the two delivery-contract docstrings

This module's docstring states a blanket assumption: "The policy assumes at-least-once delivery... Handlers observe duplicate deliveries under this contract." Read against the queue consumer's docstring ("a crash between ack and completion loses the in-flight attempt, and the run is finalized by the reaper, not redelivered"), the two aren't actually contradicting each other about the same code path — they're each accurately describing a different failure mode and presenting it as *the* contract:

- **Explicit handler exception**, caught by `_process`'s `except Exception` block → `decide()` + `reschedule()` → run goes back to `pending` → re-leased later. This really is at-least-once, exactly as this module's docstring says.
- **Worker/process death mid-flight** (crash, kill, OOM) → nothing in this module ever runs; the reaper finds the stale `running` row later and marks it `failed` with no redelivery. This really is at-most-once, exactly as the consumer's docstring says.

So the fix isn't "one of these is wrong" — it's that each docstring states its local truth as if it were the whole system's guarantee, and neither says the guarantee is conditional on *how* the attempt failed. That ambiguity is exactly what stalled the postmortem ticket: "the ticket quotes both docstrings and stalled without a decision." Both docstrings should be edited to name the other's code path and state plainly that delivery is at-least-once for application-level failures and at-most-once for process death, with a pointer to `Reaper` for the latter.

The more urgent half of the reconciliation is this module's second claim: "Handlers observe duplicate deliveries under this contract" — stated as if that's safe by assumption. It isn't, and the postmortem proves it: billing's handler declares `idempotent = false` in the catalog, and the retry path redelivered it anyway, producing 41 duplicate ledger entries that had to be reconciled by hand — "which nothing enforces." Neither `decide()` nor `reschedule()` takes the handler's idempotency into account; they can't, since neither is passed a `HandlerRegistration` or even the handler path. Given roughly a third of registered handlers are explicitly non-idempotent, unconditionally redelivering every failed attempt is not a safe default. `decide()` (or the `_process` call site) needs to branch on `idempotent`: automatic redelivery for idempotent handlers, and something else — dead-letter, manual trigger, alert — for handlers the catalog already tells you can't tolerate a second call.

## Configuration source: no namespace plumbing exists

The attached policy table is explicitly namespace-scoped — 120 distinct `max_attempts`/`base_ms`/`cap_ms` combinations, applied "through `CRONWELL_RETRY_*` environment overrides per deployment." But look at how the policy actually gets built:

```python
@classmethod
def from_config(cls) -> "RetryPolicy":
    cfg = current_config()
    return cls(max_attempts=cfg.retry_max_attempts, ...)
```

`from_config()` takes no namespace argument, `current_config()` returns one global snapshot, and `Consumer.__init__` calls `RetryPolicy.from_config()` exactly once, building a single `RetryPolicy` reused for the process's whole lifetime — `decide()` and `reschedule()` take no namespace argument either. Nowhere in this module or in `_process` does anything look at `job["namespace"]` to pick a policy.

That means "per-namespace retry policy" can only be true if each namespace runs on its own isolated worker deployment with its own environment variables — one namespace, one set of `CRONWELL_RETRY_*` values, one process. If any deployment mixes namespaces on shared workers (nothing in `LeaseStore.lease_due_runs`, reviewed earlier, filters or partitions leases by namespace, so there's no structural guarantee against this), every job leased by that worker uses whichever single global config that process happened to start with — not its own namespace's ladder. This directly undercuts the postmortem's proposed fix: the open follow-up asks for "per-namespace cap review," but the code has no mechanism to apply a reviewed, namespace-specific cap unless the deployment topology already isolates namespaces by process. That's a load-bearing assumption that isn't stated or enforced anywhere in this module — worth confirming explicitly with whoever owns deployment config before the cap-review ticket is acted on, since the fix could be a no-op if workers are shared across namespaces.

Also worth noting: the policy is fixed at `Consumer` construction. A config change (for example, the cap fix this same postmortem is asking for) won't reach an already-running worker without a restart — `decide()` never re-reads `current_config()`.

## `preview_schedule` shows one more retry than `decide()` will ever perform

Compare the two:

```python
# decide(): ceiling for attempt_no uses exponent (attempt_no - 1), and gives up once attempt_no >= max_attempts
ceiling = min(self._cap_ms, self._base_ms * (2 ** (attempt_no - 1)))
...
if attempt_no >= self._max_attempts: give up, no ceiling computed

# preview_schedule(base_ms, cap_ms, attempts): returns `attempts` entries, n = 0..attempts-1
[min(cap_ms, base_ms * (2 ** n)) for n in range(attempts)]
```

Called with `attempts=max_attempts` — which is exactly how the attached policy table presents it (ns-01: `max_attempts=3` → 3-entry ladder `[200, 400, 800]`) — `preview_schedule` computes one ceiling per attempt, `n=0..2`. But `decide()` only ever computes a ceiling for `attempt_no = 1` and `attempt_no = 2` (using exponents 0 and 1); at `attempt_no = 3` it gives up immediately with `delay_ms=0`, never touching exponent 2. So the last entry in every namespace's preview ladder — `800` for ns-01, `12800` for the 8-attempt namespaces, and so on — is a ceiling that will never be applied in production.

This is the exact table operators are using for the postmortem's proposed "per-namespace cap review." A review built on `preview_schedule`'s output is working from a ladder that's systematically one step longer than reality, which will skew any conclusions about how long the real backoff sequence runs or how it should be recapped. Either `preview_schedule` should emit `attempts - 1` entries (matching what `decide()` actually uses before giving up), or `decide()`'s give-up boundary should change to use the full ladder — but right now the two disagree, silently, for every namespace in the table.

## Full jitter's cap doesn't scale with backlog size — the March storm, explained

The full-jitter math itself matches its docstring (`randint(0, ceiling)`, ceiling saturating at `cap_ms` for later attempts) — that part is implemented correctly. But the postmortem shows its limitation concretely: once tens of thousands of runs fail inside a short window, every one of their redelivery times is spread across at most `cap_ms` (60 s for most namespaces), independent of how many runs are in that batch. A jitter window sized for spreading out a handful of concurrent retries doesn't spread out 68k of them — the batch reconverges into "near-synchronized waves" regardless of jitter, because the spread doesn't grow with backlog size. `decide()` has no visibility into queue depth or any global backpressure signal; it computes a delay purely from `attempt_no` and static config. That's consistent with what the ticket already concludes, but worth stating plainly: no config change to `cap_ms` alone fixes this class of incident, since the mechanism has no backlog-aware term. A real fix needs either a much larger cap during degraded conditions, or a backpressure/circuit-breaker signal external to this module.

## `reschedule()` can silently fail via the dedup unique index

`reschedule()` computes `next_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc) + timedelta(milliseconds=decision.delay_ms)` and calls `runs.update(run["id"], {"state": ..., "scheduled_for": next_at, "worker_id": None})`, discarding the return value entirely. Recall from the schema: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX job_runs_dedup_idx ON job_runs (job_id, scheduled_for)`, and from the storage review, `JobRunStore.update()` catches `IntegrityError` and returns `None`.

If the computed `next_at` for this run happens to collide with `scheduled_for` on another row for the same `job_id` — for example another in-flight retry for the same job landing on the same millisecond, plausible when many attempts for one job fail in a tight window, exactly the March scenario — the `UPDATE` raises `IntegrityError`, `update()` swallows it and returns `None`, and `reschedule()` never checks that. The run's `state` was never actually moved back to `pending`; it's left wherever it was before this call (still `running`, since this is the only write meant to move it forward). Nothing logs it, no metric fires, and the run has no scheduled future delivery — it's now stuck, invisible, and won't be caught by the reaper either, since the reaper only sweeps runs whose worker has gone heartbeat-silent, not runs whose reschedule silently no-opped while the worker is alive and has moved on to its next lease. This is the same "unchecked `update()` return value" pattern flagged in the consumer review, now with a concrete trigger.

## `decide()` has an unvalidated precondition on `attempt_no`

`ceiling = min(self._cap_ms, self._base_ms * (2 ** (attempt_no - 1)))` assumes `attempt_no >= 1`. If `attempt_no` is ever `0` — plausible, since the method that's supposed to supply it, `RunAttemptStore.next_attempt_no`, doesn't exist yet per the consumer review, so its indexing convention (0- or 1-based) isn't settled anywhere — the exponent goes negative, `2 ** -1` evaluates to the float `0.5` in Python, `ceiling` becomes a float, and `self._rng.randint(0, ceiling)` raises `ValueError` (`randint` requires integer bounds). Worth adding an explicit precondition (`assert attempt_no >= 1` or a validated argument) rather than relying on every caller getting the indexing convention right by accident — especially since the one caller in this codebase is calling a method that doesn't exist yet.

## `_balance_capacity` blocks the process's only lock — this is what the trace is actually showing

```python
def _balance_capacity(self) -> None:
    ...
    if active >= capacity:
        metrics.gauge("dispatcher.saturation", active - capacity)
        self._stop.wait(self._tick_s)
```

`self._stop.wait(self._tick_s)` runs while `_loop` is still holding `self._lock` (`_balance_capacity` is called from inside `with self._lock:`). `enqueue_manual` — "a user-requested immediate run (the API calls this)" — needs that same lock. So whenever the fleet is saturated, the dispatcher sits inside the lock for up to a full tick interval, and every manual-trigger API call made during that window queues up behind it.

The trace confirms this pattern precisely: the long-lock-hold ticks (t+5, 90, 175, 260, 345, 430, 515, 600, 685, 770, 855, 940, 1025) recur **every 85 seconds, exactly** — a fixed period, not noise — and each one pairs a `lock_held_s` close to `tick_s` (2.8–4.8s against a 5.0s tick) with `trigger_calls_waiting` jumping from 0 to 2–7. That's the signature of a bounded in-lock sleep, not a scan getting slower.

The trace's own note attributes this to "full-table scans of the schedules store," but the data doesn't support that: `schedules_scanned` barely moves tick to tick (40,950–41,049, under 0.3% variation), while `lock_held_s` swings by more than 10x. If scan cost were the driver, the two would track together — they don't. The regular 85-second period and the exact correlation with `trigger_calls_waiting` point at `_balance_capacity`'s saturation branch, not `_materialize_due`'s scan. Worth confirming with per-function timing before acting on the trace's note, since it's currently misattributing the cause.

Either way, the fix is the same: back off outside the lock, not inside it. A user who clicks "run now" during a saturation window has no reason to wait multiple seconds on a lock held by unrelated internal throttling.

Related: `_balance_capacity`'s docstring says it "refuses new materialization when the fleet is saturated," but by the time it runs, `_materialize_due()` has already unconditionally inserted this tick's due runs — the order in `_loop` is `_materialize_due()` then `_balance_capacity()`. The saturation check can't refuse anything on the current tick; it only delays the start of the *next* tick (and it does that by blocking the shared lock, per above). The docstring overstates what the function does.

## `_materialize_due` uses a different, and differently-typed, time source than its own horizon check

```python
now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)          # aware
horizon = now + timedelta(seconds=self._tick_s * 2)   # aware
for schedule in self._schedules.list():
    fire_at = next_run_at_from_row(schedule)          # see below
    if fire_at > horizon:
        continue
```

`next_run_at_from_row` calls `next_run_at(Schedule.from_row(schedule_row))` with no `after` argument. In `models.py`, `next_run_at(schedule, after=None)` defaults to `anchor = after or datetime.utcnow()` — and `datetime.utcnow()` is naive. Every `minute` derived from that anchor stays naive, so `fire_at` comes back with no `tzinfo`.

`fire_at > horizon` then compares a naive datetime against the aware `horizon` computed two lines above. In Python this raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes` — this isn't a subtle drift, it's an exception on the very first schedule of every tick, which `_loop`'s blanket `except Exception` would swallow into a `dispatcher.tick_error` count with zero schedules materialized.

I'll flag directly that this conflicts with what the trace shows: the trace has `_materialize_due` running to completion and successfully materializing runs every tick, which shouldn't be possible if this comparison always raises. Worth checking whether the trace was captured against this exact revision of the file — if it was, something outside what I can see here (a monkeypatch, a different `next_run_at` in play, or a modified `_materialize_due`) must be avoiding this path, and that's worth tracking down. As written, though, this is the same naive/aware gap flagged in the `models.py` review, and here it has a concrete, reachable crash site rather than a theoretical one.

Independent of whether it crashes outright: if the naive `fire_at` does get used downstream (for example if the comparison is ever "fixed" by dropping tzinfo rather than by fixing `next_run_at`), it also gets passed into `self._runs.list(job_id=..., scheduled_for=fire_at)` for the dedup check and into `JobRun(scheduled_for=fire_at, ...)` for the insert — both against a `timestamptz` column. A naive value there is subject to the same session-timezone interpretation risk raised in the storage-module review, which could make the dedup lookup miss rows that were correctly stored as aware UTC by a different code path.

## One bad schedule can silently stop materialization for the entire fleet, permanently

```python
for schedule in self._schedules.list():
    fire_at = next_run_at_from_row(schedule)
    ...
```

There's no per-schedule `try`/`except` in this loop — any exception from `next_run_at_from_row` propagates out of `_materialize_due`, is caught by `_loop`'s blanket handler, and aborts the *entire* tick. Every other schedule that tick — all ~41,000 of them — gets skipped, not just the offending one.

This interacts badly with a bug already flagged in `models.py`: `next_run_at` only scans forward 366×24×60 minutes (one year) before raising `ValidationError` if nothing matches. A legitimate cron expression that only fires on February 29 can easily have its next occurrence more than a year away (for example, right after Feb 29, 2024, the next is Feb 29, 2028 — about 1,460 days out). For three years out of four, evaluating that schedule raises `ValidationError`. Since that schedule doesn't get removed by anything, it raises on this exact code path every single tick, forever, taking down materialization for every other schedule in the system with it — a single leap-day cron entry is enough to silently halt the whole fleet's scheduling. This needs per-schedule error isolation at minimum (log and skip the one schedule, don't abort the tick), and ideally a fix to `next_run_at`'s one-year bound so a valid but rare cron expression doesn't raise at all.

## `_materialize_due` scans the whole schedules table every 5 seconds

`self._schedules.list()` takes no filter and (per the storage-module review) has no pagination — it's a full, unfiltered read of all ~41,000 rows, every tick, computing a potentially expensive `next_run_at` cron evaluation for each one even though only a handful are ever due (the trace shows `due` values of 0–35 against `schedules_scanned` of ~41,000). There's no index or query that narrows this to "schedules whose next fire time might fall in the horizon" — that computation only exists in Python. This scales linearly with total schedule count regardless of load, and it's happening under the process's only lock every tick; worth a follow-up on whether a materialized "next fire time" column, refreshed lazily, could turn this into an indexed range query instead of a full scan.

## The stated error contract doesn't match what storage actually returns

The docstring is explicit: "Storage returning `None` maps to 404." But per the storage-layer review, `insert()` and `update()` return `None` specifically when they catch `IntegrityError` — which covers unique violations, foreign-key violations, `NOT NULL` violations, and check violations alike. None of those mean "the resource is missing." Two concrete breakages follow directly from that collapse:

- **`create()` mapping a constraint failure to 404 is backwards.** `POST /api/v1/jobs` with a duplicate name hits `IntegrityError` → `insert()` returns `None` → the handler returns `{"error": "job not found"}` with status 404. There's no "job" the client asked to find — this is a brand-new resource that failed to be created because it collides with an existing one. That's a 409 (or 422), not a 404. The same applies to a `POST /api/v1/schedules` whose `job_id` doesn't reference a real job (an FK violation): the client gets "schedule not found," which doesn't even name the field that's actually wrong.
- **`update()` conflates "no such row" with "your change is invalid."** `PATCH /api/v1/jobs/5` to rename a job to a name that collides with another job's unique constraint returns exactly the same `{"error": "job not found"}` as patching an id that was deleted yesterday. A client that just successfully `GET`'d job 5 moments earlier will be told it doesn't exist. The single bit of signal storage exposes (`None` vs. not-`None`) can't carry the distinction this docstring promises. Fixing this needs `insert`/`update` in the storage layer to distinguish constraint-violation subtypes (or at minimum re-raise a typed error the API layer can branch on) rather than collapsing everything to `None`.

## `update()`'s `changes` dict is unvalidated, client-controlled, and goes straight into SQL

This is the most severe issue in the file. The storage review flagged that `update()`'s `SET {key} = %s` clause is built from `changes`' keys with no allow-list, unlike `list()`, which does validate filter keys against known columns. Here, `changes = request.json()` is **raw JSON from the HTTP request body**, passed straight to `self._store.update(id, changes)` with no key validation of any kind:

- Nothing strips `id` from `changes` (contrast with `list()`'s explicit `if key != "id"` filtering of query params). A client can `PATCH /api/v1/jobs/5` with `{"id": 999}` and the resulting SQL is `UPDATE jobs SET id = %s WHERE id = %s` — a client-driven primary-key rewrite.
- More seriously, since the *column name* itself is spliced into the SQL text (`f"{key} = %s"`) rather than parameterized, a JSON body with a crafted key — not a value, a *key* — is embedded literally into the query. `%s` placeholders protect values; they do nothing for identifiers. This is a live, HTTP-reachable SQL injection path through every single `update()` endpoint in this file (all ten resource classes), not a theoretical one.

This needs the same fix `list()` already has: validate `changes`' keys against the resource's known column set before building the `SET` clause, and explicitly reject `id`.

## Every `id`-taking handler can throw an unhandled exception instead of a documented response

`get`, `update`, `delete`, `cancel`, `trigger`, and `tail` all do `int(request.params["id"])` with no guard, outside any `try`/`except`:

- Missing `id` param → `KeyError`, uncaught.
- Non-numeric `id` (`"abc"`) → `ValueError`, uncaught.

The docstring's contract only names three outcomes: 404, 422, and auth (handled by middleware). A bad `id` produces none of these — it produces whatever the surrounding framework does with an unhandled exception, presumably a 500 with no `Response.invalid`-style message. This is the same gap repeated at every one of these call sites across all ten resource classes plus `RunControlHandlers`; worth factoring into one small helper that catches the conversion and returns `Response.invalid(...)`.

## `list()` endpoints have no pagination, and `tail()` is the clearest case of it mattering

Every `list()` handler forwards straight to `self._store.list(**filters)`, which (per the storage review) has no `LIMIT`/offset/cursor support — it returns every matching row, fully materialized, serialized whole into the response body. Given the dispatcher trace showed ~41,000 rows in the schedules table alone, and `job_runs`/`run_attempts`/`audit_events` are append-heavy history tables that only grow (nothing reviewed so far purges them despite `Namespace.retention_days` existing as a field), `GET /api/v1/job_runs` or `GET /api/v1/audit_events` with **no filters at all** returns the entire table in one response. That's an availability risk on its own.

`RunControlHandlers.tail()` makes this concrete and mislabeled:

```python
def tail(self, request: Request) -> Response:
    """The most recent runs of a job, newest first."""
    rows = self._runs.list(job_id=int(request.params["id"]))
    return Response.ok(rows[::-1])
```

"Tail" implies a bounded, recent-items view, but there's no `LIMIT` anywhere in this call — it fetches every run the job has ever had, then reverses the whole list in Python just to put it in descending order. A job that fires every minute for a year has north of 500,000 runs; this endpoint would try to return all of them. This needs a real `LIMIT` pushed to SQL (`ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT N`), not a full fetch-then-reverse.

## The public API lets clients bypass system-owned tables entirely

`JobRunHandlers`, `RunAttemptHandlers`, and `AuditEventHandlers` expose full CRUD — including `create`, `update`, and `delete` — on tables that other modules treat as system-managed records:

- `POST /api/v1/job_runs` lets a client fabricate a run in any state, including `state: "succeeded"`, without the handler ever executing — bypassing the dispatcher's materialization logic (`next_run_at`, the dedup index, capacity checks) entirely. There's already a controlled path for user-initiated runs — `RunControlHandlers.trigger()`, which correctly goes through `self._dispatcher.enqueue_manual(...)` — so the generic CRUD endpoint is a second, uncontrolled way to write the same table.
- `POST/PATCH/DELETE /api/v1/audit_events` lets any client with API access write or rewrite audit trail entries, including the `actor` field, attributing actions to whoever they choose. An audit log that any caller can freely edit isn't functioning as an audit log.

If this is meant to be a general-purpose API rather than an internal admin tool, these three resources probably shouldn't have open write access from HTTP at all — at minimum `audit_events` should be append-only-by-the-system, and `job_runs`/`run_attempts` mutation should be restricted to the components that actually own their lifecycle (dispatcher, consumer, reaper), with the public API limited to read plus the already-correct `trigger`/`cancel` verbs.

## `cancel()` doesn't reference `RunState` and doesn't actually stop anything in flight

```python
def cancel(self, request: Request) -> Response:
    row = self._runs.update(int(request.params["id"]), {"state": "dead"})
```

`RunState` isn't even imported in this file — `"dead"` is a bare string literal duplicating `RunState.DEAD.value` by coincidence rather than reference. A future rename of the enum's value wouldn't be caught here.

More importantly: if the run is currently `running` on a worker, this only rewrites the database row — nothing notifies the worker executing the handler. The consumer (reviewed earlier) has no cancellation check in its poll loop, so the handler keeps running, and when it finishes, `_process`'s own `self._runs.update(...)` for `succeeded`/`dead`/retry overwrites whatever `cancel()` just wrote, with no compare-and-swap or version check to detect the conflict. "Cancel" only reliably works for runs that are `pending` (not yet leased); for anything already in flight it's a race the API call will usually lose invisibly.

## Filter values from `list()` aren't type-checked

Query-string values in `request.params` arrive as strings. They're forwarded directly into `store.list(**filters)` with no coercion — `GET /api/v1/workers?draining=false` sends the string `"false"`, not a Python bool, to a `boolean` column, and `GET /api/v1/jobs?priority=5` sends the string `"5"` to an `integer` column. Postgres's implicit casting will likely paper over both cases in practice, but that's incidental behavior, not a contract this code establishes — worth adding explicit coercion (or documenting that filters are cast leniently) rather than relying on the database to make it work.

## Smaller items

- `Job.from_row({'id': None, **request.json()})` puts `'id': None` first and spreads the request body over it — if a client's JSON includes an `id` key (plausible if they're echoing back a fetched object to create a copy), the client's `id` wins the merge, not `None`. This happens to be harmless today only because `JobStore.insert()`'s SQL hardcodes its column list and never reads `row["id"]` — but that's an incidental safety net, not something this file arranges on purpose. Worth reordering to `{**request.json(), 'id': None}` so the intent is explicit and doesn't depend on a coincidence in a different module.
- `RunControlHandlers` (`trigger`, `cancel`, `tail`) has no `metrics.timer(...)` wrapping, unlike every CRUD handler in the other ten classes — an inconsistent observability gap on what are probably some of the more operationally important endpoints.
- No visible namespace/tenant scoping on any `get`/`list` handler — any caller that passes auth can filter or fetch across every namespace's jobs, payloads, and handler paths. If per-namespace isolation is expected (the `Namespace`/`owner_team` concept suggests it might be), it isn't enforced anywhere in this file — worth confirming whether that's intentional for what looks like an internal/admin surface.

## Config load order: the token table is frozen before the real config is read

This is the most consequential finding, and the module documents its own bug directly in the comment:

```python
# Resolved once at import: the token table and the allowlist. main()
# loads the config file after imports, so an import-time read sees
# the bootstrap defaults unless the environment overrides them.
_CONFIG = current_config()
_TOKEN_TABLE = {entry.token_sha256: entry for entry in _CONFIG.api_tokens}
_ALLOWLIST = set(_CONFIG.admin_networks or [])
```

Python resolves all module-level code — including this `current_config()` call — during the import phase, before any line of `main()` runs. If `main()`'s job is to load `cronwell.toml` from disk (the config-loader module, reviewed next, should confirm this explicitly), then by the time `main()` actually reads the real file, this module has already captured `_TOKEN_TABLE`/`_ALLOWLIST` from whatever `current_config()` returned beforehand — the comment calls this "bootstrap defaults." Unless every value this module needs is also injected through the environment (bypassing the file entirely), the running process's notion of valid tokens and admin networks is disconnected from the deployed `cronwell.toml` for its entire lifetime. This needs the load order inverted: config must be loaded before this module (or anything importing it) executes, or this module needs an explicit `init()` that `main()` calls after loading config, rather than doing the real work at import time.

The audit log's rotation-failure pattern (`unknown_token` for "token present in the NEW config file") is consistent with this bug, but I want to be precise about what it does and doesn't prove: the interleaved ok/unknown_token results across many different remote IPs in the same time window is exactly what you'd also expect from an ordinary rolling deploy where old instances (old token table) and new instances (new token table) are both serving traffic simultaneously — that pattern alone doesn't distinguish "the import-order bug" from "instances just haven't restarted yet, which is expected." Worth confirming directly (check whether *any* instance, including ones freshly restarted after the rotation, successfully authenticates the new token) rather than inferring it purely from this log.

## Decision cache: no expiry, no revocation path

```python
_DECISION_CACHE: dict[str, AuthResult] = {}
```

Once `check()` caches a decision for a token, that decision holds for the rest of the process's life — there is no TTL, no invalidation on config change, and no code path that clears it in production (`reset_for_tests()`'s own docstring says "production never does" call it). Combined with the import-time freeze above, this means revoking a compromised token — the whole point of a token-based access system — doesn't actually take effect until every process in the fleet is restarted. For a security control, "revocation requires a full fleet restart, and even then only works if the restart timing wins the race against the import-order bug" is a serious gap worth fixing directly: either cache with a short TTL, or key the cache off something that changes when config reloads, or don't cache negative/no-longer-valid decisions past a bounded window.

## Cache key omits `remote_addr` — this breaks the admin IP allowlist

```python
cached = _DECISION_CACHE.get(token)
if cached is not None:
    return cached
...
elif entry.role == "admin" and _ALLOWLIST and remote_addr not in _ALLOWLIST:
    result = AuthResult(False)
else:
    result = AuthResult(True, team=entry.team, role=entry.role)
_DECISION_CACHE[token] = result
```

The allowlist decision depends on `remote_addr`, but the cache is keyed only by `token`. The first time an admin token is used from an address inside the allowlist, `AuthResult(True, ...)` gets cached under that token — and every later request presenting the *same token from any address*, including ones outside `_ALLOWLIST`, hits the cache and returns the cached `True` without the allowlist ever being re-checked. Any admin token that has ever successfully authenticated once from an allowed network — which will happen routinely in normal operation — can then be replayed from anywhere, completely bypassing the network restriction. This is a genuine authorization bypass, not just a staleness issue.

It also causes the opposite failure: if an admin token's *first* use in a process happens to come from outside the allowlist (a stray probe, a misrouted request, anything), the resulting `AuthResult(False)` gets cached and permanently blocks that token for the rest of the process's life, even for later legitimate calls from inside the allowed networks. Either way, caching a decision that depends on a per-request value (`remote_addr`) under a key that doesn't include that value is the root problem — the fix is either keying the cache by `(token, remote_addr)` or excluding the allowlist branch from caching altogether and re-evaluating it every request.

## The admin allowlist doesn't do CIDR matching at all

```python
_ALLOWLIST = set(_CONFIG.admin_networks or [])   # e.g. {"10.8.0.0/24", "10.9.4.0/24"}
...
elif entry.role == "admin" and _ALLOWLIST and remote_addr not in _ALLOWLIST:
```

`admin_networks` in the config is CIDR notation. `remote_addr` is a concrete client address like `10.8.6.82`. `remote_addr not in _ALLOWLIST` is a plain set-membership string comparison — `"10.8.6.82"` will never equal the string `"10.8.0.0/24"`, no matter how the network is configured. There's no use of `ipaddress.ip_network(...)`/containment logic anywhere in this file. Two outcomes follow, and they're both bad:

- If `_ALLOWLIST` is populated (non-empty), `remote_addr not in _ALLOWLIST` is `True` for every real client address, so **every admin-role request is rejected, unconditionally, from any source IP** — the control doesn't restrict admin access to trusted networks, it blocks it entirely.
- If `_ALLOWLIST` is empty — which, tying back to the import-order bug above, would happen if the import-time "bootstrap defaults" snapshot doesn't include `admin_networks` even though the real `cronwell.toml` does — the `and _ALLOWLIST and ...` short-circuits false, and the restriction is **silently skipped entirely**: any IP can use a valid admin token with no network restriction at all.

I can't tell from the attached log which state production is currently in — no `admin_outside_allowlist` result appears anywhere in the excerpt, which is at least consistent with the second (silent-bypass) case, since a total-lockout failure mode would likely have already been noticed and escalated as "we can't do any admin operations." Worth confirming directly: check the current value of `_ALLOWLIST` in a running process and the `auth.admin_outside_allowlist` metric's history. Either way, this needs real CIDR containment logic (`ipaddress.ip_address(remote_addr) in ipaddress.ip_network(cidr)` for each entry), not set membership.

## Unbounded cache growth is a memory-exhaustion vector

`_DECISION_CACHE` has no size limit and no eviction. Every distinct bearer token string ever presented — including outright garbage from an attacker probing the endpoint — gets a permanent entry, since `check()` caches `AuthResult(False)` for unknown tokens exactly the same way it caches valid ones. A client (malicious or just misbehaving) sending many distinct invalid tokens grows this dict without bound for the life of the process, with no rate limiting anywhere in this module to slow that down. This needs a bounded cache (LRU with a max size, or a TTL) rather than a plain unbounded dict.

## Cache stores plaintext tokens, not digests

The cache key is the raw bearer token string, even though the module already computes `hashlib.sha256(token.encode()).hexdigest()` for the actual lookup. Keying the cache by the digest instead would avoid holding every presented token's plaintext in a long-lived process-wide dictionary, reducing exposure if process memory is ever inspected (core dump, debug endpoint, etc.) — a small change with a real reduction in blast radius for a module whose entire job is guarding secrets.

## Smaller items

- On a cache hit, `check()` returns before ever calling `_lookup`/`hmac.compare_digest` — so the constant-time comparison only protects the *first* request for a given token in a process's life; every subsequent request for that same token goes through a plain dict `.get()`. `models.py` defines `DEFAULT_RETRY_BACKOFF_BASE_MS = 250`. `config_loader.py`'s bootstrap default is `retry_backoff_base_ms: int = 200`. Normally this is masked: the deployed `cronwell.toml` sets `[retry] backoff_base_ms = 250`, which (once loaded) overrides the bootstrap default and matches `models.py`. But the effective-config diff shows exactly the failure mode where the drift becomes visible: `retry_backoff_base_ms | 250 | 250 | 200` — scheduler-3 is running with the bootstrap default, not the file's value, because (per the next finding) its `load()` never actually read the file. ## Reconsidering the auth-middleware finding: `load()` can never reach a module that already grabbed `current_config()`

Now that `load()`'s implementation is visible, the earlier auth-middleware concern is stronger than "an ordering coincidence" — it's structural:

```python
def load(path=None) -> Config:
    global _current
    ...
    _current = Config(api_tokens=tokens, **values)   # rebinds the name
    return _current
```

`load()` doesn't mutate the existing `Config` object — `Config` is frozen, so it can't. It creates a brand-new `Config` and **rebinds the module-level name** `_current` to point at it. `auth_middleware.py` does this at its own import time:

```python
_CONFIG = current_config()
_TOKEN_TABLE = {entry.token_sha256: entry for entry in _CONFIG.api_tokens}
```

`_CONFIG` holds a direct reference to whatever `Config` object `current_config()` returned *at that moment*. It is not a pointer to `config_loader._current` — it's a copy of one specific reference. When `load()` later rebinds `config_loader._current` to a new object, `auth_middleware._CONFIG` keeps pointing at the old one. There is no mechanism by which `load()` can reach back and update it — not a race, not a timing issue that resolves itself once things settle, but a permanent disconnection for the rest of that process's life, guaranteed by how Python name binding works. The only way `auth_middleware._CONFIG` would ever reflect a loaded file is if `auth_middleware` happened to be imported *after* `main()` already called `load()` — a fragile ordering that isn't documented or enforced, and isn't how Python programs are normally structured (imports resolve before `main()`'s body runs).

This also means the effective-config diff table doesn't tell you what auth is actually enforcing. `/configz` renders `dump_effective(current_config())` — it reads `config_loader._current` live, at request time, so it correctly reflects the *loader's* current state. `auth_middleware.py` never calls `current_config()` again after its one-time import. These are two independent snapshots. Scheduler-1 and scheduler-2 showing "24 tokens" on `/configz` is not evidence that `auth_middleware` on those instances is checking requests against 24 tokens — it only proves `config_loader._current` has 24 tokens. Whatever `auth_middleware._TOKEN_TABLE` actually contains on any of these three instances is invisible from this diff entirely. Given the June rotation log already showed real `unknown_token` failures for tokens that were present in the newly-deployed file, that's independent evidence this disconnection is a real, live problem, not just a theoretical one. I'd recommend exposing `len(_TOKEN_TABLE)` from `auth_middleware` itself on `/configz` (or an equivalent diagnostic), because right now ops can look at a reassuring "24 tokens" and have no idea the auth path is running on something else entirely.

## `load()` fails silently when there's no file to read

```python
if path is not None and Path(path).exists():
    with open(path, "rb") as handle:
        raw = tomllib.load(handle)
    values.update(_flatten(raw))
values.update(_environment_overrides())
...
_current = Config(api_tokens=tokens, **values)
```

If `path` is `None`, or points at a file that doesn't exist (yet, or ever), this whole block is skipped — no exception, no log line, nothing. `load()` just proceeds to build a `Config` from bootstrap defaults plus whatever's in the environment, and returns it as if it were a normal, successful load. There's no way for a caller to distinguish "loaded the real file" from "the file wasn't there and I quietly used defaults."

The effective-config diff shows this happening on scheduler-3 right now: `api_tokens | <0 tokens>`, `admin_networks | ()`, `retry_backoff_base_ms | 200` — all bootstrap defaults, not the file's values, on an instance where `load()` is confirmed to have run ("its `/configz` shows `load()` ran"). Zero API tokens means every real client request to that instance fails auth; empty `admin_networks` means (per the prior turn's finding) the admin-network restriction is silently disabled entirely, should any token happen to authenticate. This needs `load()` to fail loudly — raise, or at minimum log an error — when `path` is `None` or doesn't resolve to a real file, rather than treating that as an unremarkable, successful path.

## `[defaults]` is completely non-functional — a real, currently-masked landing bug

The loader note invites verifying that each TOML section actually lands on its `Config` field. Walking every section against `_flatten`'s logic, every one composes correctly except this one:

```toml
[defaults]
priority = 5
jitter_s = 30
```

`_flatten` tries `f"{section}_{key}"` first: `"defaults_priority"` and `"defaults_jitter_s"`. Neither matches an actual field — the `Config` fields are `default_priority` and `default_jitter_s` (singular "default", not "defaults"). It then falls back to the bare key (`"priority"`, `"jitter_s"`), which also doesn't match any field. Both settings are silently dropped, every time, and `default_priority`/`default_jitter_s` always take the Python bootstrap default (5 and 30) instead.

This is currently invisible because the TOML's values (5, 30) happen to equal the bootstrap defaults exactly. If anyone edits `[defaults] priority = 10` in the file expecting it to take effect, it won't — silently, with no error, forever, until someone notices `default_priority` never changes no matter what the file says. This needs either the TOML section renamed to `[default]` or the `Config` fields renamed to `defaults_priority`/`defaults_jitter_s` to match.

## The composed-name/bare-key fallback is a cross-section collision hazard

`lease_batch` currently lands correctly, but only via the bare-key fallback (`"dispatcher_lease_batch"` isn't a field, so it falls back to `"lease_batch"`, which is). That means any *other* section that also happens to use a bare key `lease_batch` — or any bare key that doesn't compose into a known field name — would land in the exact same flat dict slot and silently overwrite whichever section's block was processed later, since Python dict iteration order follows the TOML's own key order and nothing detects the collision. This works today only because no other section happens to reuse a colliding bare key. Worth hardening `_flatten` to reject (or at least warn on) ambiguous bare-key fallbacks rather than relying on this being a coincidence of the current file.
